articles.title: Trump mourns Florida detective killed by suspected drunk driver on Thanksgiving
articles.summary: President Donald Trump paid tribute to Palm Beach County Detective Alan Smith, a bomb squad expert killed in a wrong-way crash on I-95 on Thanksgiving.
articles.body: President Donald Trump paid tribute Thursday to a Florida sheriff's detective killed in a wrong-way crash involving a suspected drunk driver on Thanksgiving morning. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office identified the fallen officer as Detective Alan Smith, who had served with the department for nearly 20 years. Smith, who specialized in explosives-related investigations, was fatally struck by a wrong-way driver on Interstate 95 early Thursday morning, according to the sheriff's office. "It is with profound sadness and heavy hearts that we announce the devastating loss [of] our own, Detective Alan Smith," the department said in a statement. DRUNK WRONG-WAY DRIVER KILLED MASS TROOPER AFTER 9 DRINKS AT BAR, DA REPORT SAYS Speaking Thursday during an event at Mar-a-Lago, Trump paid his respects to the family of the fallen officer, whom he described as "highly respected." "I just want to pay my respects to the family of a great police officer, an expert at bombs and explosives, who was killed today in an automobile accident while on duty," Trump said. Trump described the crash as "horrific," saying the other driver had been traveling in the wrong direction on Interstate 95. "It was a drunk driver. Really drunk driver," Trump said. "He was going on the opposite side of the highway, if you can believe it. And so it's a terrible thing that happened." The Florida Highway Patrol arrested Raul Jonathan Espinoza Martinez, 37, Thursday afternoon at St. Mary's Medical Center in West Palm Beach. SUSPECT IN DEADLY PHILADELPHIA POLICE AMBUSH FACES 76 CHARGES, ORDERED HELD WITHOUT BAIL Troopers were joined by members of the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office, who placed Martinez in the same handcuffs carried by Smith. Martinez is expected to be booked into the Palm Beach County Jail once he is released from the hospital. He faces multiple charges, including DUI manslaughter, vehicular homicide, aggravated battery, aggravated battery on a law enforcement officer and driving with a suspended or revoked license. Authorities said Martinez has been arrested three times for DUI and that his driver's license had been revoked for 10 years, according to local outlet CBS12. "This is a tragedy that shouldn't have happened," Florida Highway Patrol Maj. Kevin Strickland said. "He shouldn't have been driving a car at all, so part of our investigation is gonna determine how he was driving the car he was driving and how he got access to that vehicle." ALLEGED DRUNKEN DRIVER WAS OVER 3 TIMES THE LIMIT WHEN HE KILLED NEWLY ENGAGED WOMAN DAYS AFTER JAIL RELEASE Smith joined the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office in January 2007 before becoming a member of its bomb squad in 2012 and graduating from the FBI Hazardous Devices School in September 2013. He also served as a task force officer with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), specializing in explosives-related investigations. Beyond his law enforcement career, Smith was a college professor and was working toward completing his doctoral degree, according to the sheriff's office. He is survived by his wife, Jennifer, and their 14-year-old son, Alexander. "Above all his professional and academic accomplishments, Alan's greatest pride was his family," the sheriff's office said. THE FBI IS CHANGING HOW IT FIGHTS CRIME AND PROTECTS AMERICANS IN THEIR COMMUNITIES Tributes poured in from across the country, including from FBI Director Kash Patel. "Detective Smith was one of the FBI's own, having graduated from the FBI Hazardous Devices School in September 2013," Patel wrote on X, adding that Smith had "a long decorated career of service to this country." "This is yet another reminder of the sacrifices our law enforcement make standing their posts even on holidays to keep us safe," he added. "Never forget them and their families. Our prayers are with Detective Smith's wife and 14 year old son, as well as the colleagues he leaves behind." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Rep. Byron Donalds, R-Fla., Florida's governor-elect, also reacted to Smith's death, calling the news "devastating." "This is a sober and heartbreaking reminder of the dangers that our brave law enforcement officers face day in and day out as they risk everything to keep us safe," he posted on X.

articles.title: Old wounds reopen as Kyrgyzstan’s Osh embraces a new urban project
articles.summary: Redevelopment reshapes the city, but some worry as residents are displaced and cultural heritage appears at risk.
articles.body:
Osh, Kyrgyzstan – Kyrgyzstan’s second-largest city is in the throes of a major regeneration programme.

New IT hubs are planned for Osh, as well as apartments, schools and nurseries. Transport projects, a waste-to-energy plant and a livestock complex are being worked on too. A “modern school” for 530 children, kitted out with solar panels, was completed in 10 months and will open in the coming days.

But several hundred homes have been demolished to make way for new infrastructure, stirring fears about the future and the character of the old city.

The fast-paced campaign to modernise could also affect Osh’s mountain of Sulaiman-Too – a UNESCO World Heritage site.

Osh lies just 5km from the border with Uzbekistan and is home to about 485,000 people – about 40 percent are Uzbek.

Kyrgyz authorities in the town “want to erase us from the history of this city”, said 84-year-old Mogamed Kambarow, an Uzbek with a white beard and sun-bronzed face. In March, about a third of his home was destroyed as municipal authorities worked to widen Alisher Navoi Street.

“They sent bulldozers, pulled down the walls and left,” said Kambarow, who was at home at the time. He received no compensation and lives in the remaining parts.

Neighbours alerted each other when the demolition began. An 11-year-old girl was injured by falling bricks and taken to hospital, he said.

Kambarow’s memories haunt him. He was around when violence engulfed the city before.

In 2010, inter-communal tensions spilled over into violence. More than 400 people were killed and thousands of homes were destroyed. Most of the victims were ethnic Uzbeks.

In 1990, shortly before the collapse of the Soviet Union, as Uzbeks demanded more autonomy and as land disputes raged, fighting and riots broke out between the two groups and hundreds were killed.

‘It isn’t only Uzbek property that is damaged’

But Gulgaky Mamasalieva, head of the International Centre Interbilim, an organisation in Osh that provides legal help to residents today, says the current redevelopment affects everyone.

“It isn’t only Uzbek property that is damaged,” she told Al Jazeera, adding that more than 750 households were affected by the latest demolitions, including many Kyrgyz families.

According to a report by Interbilim, 65 percent of households first learned that their homes were going to be demolished when city workers painted the Russian word snos, meaning “demolition”, on their walls.

Some residents received letters telling them to leave within three days. Others, like those on Navoi Street, were visited by the mayor, who announced the plans himself.

“But people expected that there would be some paperwork done first,” said Mamasalieva.

Osh sits at the eastern end of the Ferghana Valley, the agricultural heart of Central Asia. The area is divided between three former Soviet republics: Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan.

Historically, Osh had a predominantly Uzbek population. During the Soviet national delimitation of Central Asia in the 1920s, the city was incorporated into the Kyrgyz Soviet republic.

In those days, the whole city used to look like the quarters along Navoi Street, where flat-roofed houses hide behind high fences and yards full of grapevines offer some shade from the scorching sun. These areas are known as “mahallas” – an old word for an administrative and community unit.

As the years passed, a university was established, factories built, and the population grew.

Just behind Kambarow’s house, a path leads up Sulaiman-Too. The mountain is a holy site for Muslims and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2009.

It is believed that the ancient Greek geographer Ptolemy mentioned the mountain in his book Geography. Babur, who was born in the Ferghana Valley and later founded the Mughal Empire, built a house of prayer on its summit.

The building was destroyed during a Soviet campaign against religion in the 1960s, but rebuilt in the late 1980s. Some Muslims believe that visiting Sulaiman-Too three times is equal to making one pilgrimage to Mecca.

There are also three cemeteries on the mountain where old gravestones rise from the long grass.

Retired pilot Abduraim Amanbaev, 73, climbs Sulaiman-Too every Friday, after prayers. He takes a shortcut through the cemetery to avoid paying the entrance fee, as the mountain is also a tourist attraction.

“The oldest grave dates back to the 14th century,” Amanbaev said.

His family home has been destroyed three times during his lifetime. The first time was in the 1960s, when the Soviet authorities modernised the city. The second was in 2010, during the ethnic violence. Now, it is happening again. “People are tired,” he said. Half of his house was destroyed. He lives in the other half and has not been compensated.

Mamasalieva from Interbilim told Al Jazeera that the city was supposed to agree on compensation with each household before demolishing their property. Disputes should have gone to court. While they received guarantee papers signed electronically by the vice-mayor, the documents did not detail compensation packages, she said.

Only families whose houses were completely destroyed were offered new flats. More than 100 households were moved to Ene-Say, a residential area 10km (6 miles) outside Osh. Another 64 families were given flats in an apartment block in the city.

But for some, relocation has caused further problems.

“We still haven’t been given the deeds for this flat,” said a 37-year-old woman who now lives in Ene-Say, who requested anonymity.

Without official ownership, her family cannot register their new address or access free healthcare and other services. Some families said they have also been asked to pay the government the difference between the value of their old homes and their new flats.

Interbilim said it is ready to help residents take the authorities to court, but so far nobody has been willing to do so.

“The city promised that anyone who wanted to open a business along Navoi Street would be given permission,” said Mamasalieva.

Osh’s debts total up to 3 billion soms ($34m), according to Kyrgyz media. City authorities rejected that figure when contacted by Al Jazeera, saying the budget for this year is 5.2 billion soms ($57m). Officials did not respond to questions regarding the backlash over the development plans.

Sulaiman-Too is a key source of tourism income. It attracts about 370,000 visitors each year, according to Hairullo Ibaydullaev, a deputy director of the National Historical and Archaeological Museum Complex Sulayman, which is carved inside the mountain.

Renovation across the mountain began in October. The plans include improving the footpaths, replacing lighting and building a car park. The $12m project is being funded by the World Bank and is expected to take one year.

But Ibaydullaev said the mountain is under pressure from developers who want to use the surrounding land, even though it is protected by UNESCO. The mountain has a buffer zone covering 4,788 hectares (11,830 acres), which includes Navoi Street.

City officials say these restrictions make it harder to develop Osh.

Sabira Soltongeldieva, head of the National Commission of the Kyrgyz Republic for UNESCO, said that Bishkek has asked to reconsider how the buffer zone is used.

The former mayor, Jenishbek Toktorboev, asked the Ministry of Culture to release some of the protected land for new projects. He earned the nickname “Demolition Uncle” among some after he ordered the destruction of the old Jayma Bazaar, once the city’s main trading centres.

“The vendors were given 15 days to disappear,” said a knife-maker, whose stall was one of those allowed to remain.

Toktorboev also began building apartment blocks at the foot of the mountain, taller than the rules for the buffer zone allowed. He wanted to remove one of the three cemeteries and build a leisure park in its place. This project failed. Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov dismissed him in February.

The new mayor, Janar Akaev, has continued to propose new developments.

In August, Akaev announced plans to build a cable car to the top of the mountain, comparing it to those in Switzerland.

He also announced a plan to remove the mountain from the UNESCO World Heritage list – a proposal rejected by the culture ministry.

“This is the most complete example of a sacred mountain in Central Asia,” said Ibaydullaev.

articles.title: Italians killed in Kuwait: Why is Iran denying responsibility?
articles.summary: Iran has openly claimed its strikes on Gulf states throughout the war. So why is it denying an attack on Kuwait?
articles.body:
Two Italian technicians were killed in a drone attack on a military site in Kuwait on Thursday, the first European civilians to die amid the United States-Israel war on Iran.

The victims were named by Italian media as Antonio Saccoccio, 65, from Formia, and Emanuele Lo Russo, 36, from Rome. They were maintaining detection antennae for the Skyguard air defence system used by Kuwait’s armed forces.

Kuwait and Italy blamed Iran. Tehran, which has for the most part not denied, outright, strikes on US military assets hosted by its Gulf neighbours and described those attacks as self-defence, has this time denied any role and has suggested the strike was a “false-flag” operation.

The denial has raised two questions: Who was behind the attack and, if it was Iran, why is it not taking responsibility?

On Thursday, several drones targeted military installations in Kuwait, according to Italy’s Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani.

Kuwait’s army initially described the target only as a “vital site”. Tajani later told the Italian Senate that it included an air-defence detection station where two technicians from Rheinmetall Italia, the Italian arm of the German defence company, were working.

They were killed by falling shrapnel after the drones were intercepted, according to Kuwaiti and Italian reports. A Kuwaiti and a Pakistani national were injured.

The two dead men are the first European civilians to be killed as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran since it began in late February. A French soldier was killed in a drone attack in Iraq in March.

This was the first fatal strike on Kuwait in several months, although the country has been one of the hardest-hit Gulf states during the war. Its oil facilities, power infrastructure and airport have all been targeted at various points in the conflict. An Indian traveller was killed and 63 people were injured when drones hit Kuwait international airport on June 3 .

Iran said it last struck Kuwait on November 18 .

What have Kuwait and Italy said about the latest incident?

Both countries have blamed Iran for Thursday’s drone strike.

Kuwait’s Foreign Ministry condemned what it called a “sinful” attack and said the country reserved its right to take all measures to protect its sovereignty and the security of its citizens and residents.

After a call between Kuwait’s foreign minister and Tajani, the Kuwaiti ministry said the two had jointly condemned the strike.

Tajani told the Italian parliament the drones were “of Iranian origin”. The Gulf Cooperation Council’s secretary-general, Jasem Albudaiwi, also condemned what he called a “brutal attack”.

“The incident is suspicious and looks like a pre-cooked recipe for war,” Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X.

Araghchi called both his Kuwaiti and Italian counterparts to deny Iranian involvement and offered to mount a joint investigation, according to Iran’s foreign ministry. As of Thursday evening, Kuwait had not publicly commented on the call with Araghchi.

Armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi, speaking for both the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the regular army, said Iranian forces had conducted “no military or offensive operations whatsoever” in the region. He called the attack a “false flag” operation, while a military statement accused the US and Israel of using it as cover for continued aggression.

The Iranian embassy in Rome said it “categorically rejects the allegation”, suggesting the attack could have been staged to drag Europe into the Iran war.

The denial stands out because Iran has rarely disowned its attacks since US-Israeli strikes began in February. In November alone, it issued five statements claiming strikes on neighbouring states, four of them on Bahrain and Kuwait.

Tehran usually tries to justify those strikes as self-defence, arguing that it targets US bases from which Iran is attacked, not the countries that host them.

This is not the first time Iran has denied an attack on Kuwait, however. When a power and desalination plant was hit on March 30 , killing an Indian worker, Iran also claimed that Israel was responsible.

What do we know about who launched the drones?

Hassan Ahmadian, a professor of Middle East studies at the University of Tehran, said Iran’s record of claiming its strikes should be taken seriously.

“Whenever the Iranians do something, they announce it,” he told Al Jazeera. “This time, as on three or four occasions during the war, they said, ‘This wasn’t us.'”

He argued that Iran would have little reason to hide this attack. “They’ve struck the Americans,” he said. “Would they be afraid to announce they’d hit Italians?”

Ahmadian said other parties in the region, such as Israel, might want to “complicate the situation” by blaming Iran, which he called “the ready-made party to blame”. He added that some in Iran also suspect Ukraine, which he argued has been trying to raise its strategic value to Washington.

As the US ran down its stock of expensive Patriot missile interceptor systems against a barrage of cheap, mass-produced Iranian Shahed drones, Ukraine offered its expertise to the US in March on how to combat the drones, which are also used by Russia.

Ahmadian said US involvement could not be ruled out either. Iran has previously told regional governments that the US was behind strikes on two sites during the war, he said.

“We’re looking at someone fishing in troubled waters. Otherwise, if it were the Iranians, they would have announced it,” he added.

Paolo von Schirach, president of the Global Policy Institute and a professor of political science at Bay Atlantic University in Washington, dismissed the idea of US involvement.

“It’s bizarre to suggest the United States would coordinate this attack on Kuwait, an ally in the Gulf, just to stir up feelings,” he said.

Von Schirach noted that Italy has refused to join the US war on Iran and does not support it. “Italy isn’t on America’s side in this conflict,” he said. “So we shouldn’t take this seriously.”

Muhanad Seloom, a senior non-resident fellow at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, said it was important to “separate Iranian-made from Iranian-launched and Iranian-ordered”.

Tajani described the drone as Iranian-built, of a type also used by Iran-backed militias. Seloom said that makes an Iraqi armed faction the leading alternative suspect. Such groups have claimed attacks on US forces in Gulf states since the war began.

He called Yemen’s Houthis “a distant second” and said Tehran’s own suspects, the US, Israel and Ukraine, “come with no evidence”.

“Only debris, radar tracks and a launch point can settle it,” he told Al Jazeera.

Seloom said Tehran first used it in March over strikes on Turkiye, Cyprus and Azerbaijan . However, he said that The Soufan Center, a US-based security think tank, found that it failed to convince Baku.

Claims have run the other way, too. The best known was the reported arrest of Mossad agents plotting bombings in Qatar and Saudi Arabia, which came to nothing, Seloom said, because neither of those governments stood behind it.

“Alleged often, verified never, as far as I can establish,” he said. “What this war has is deniable action. Hiding the author is common. Framing someone else has yet to be shown.”

In the case of Thursday’s attack, he said, Iran’s false-flag claim “stands without evidence so far”.

Abdullah al-Shayji, a professor of political science at Kuwait University, said Iran’s narrative “doesn’t come close to being rational or acceptable”.

“Iran bombed us eight days ago, on the 18th of this month, and didn’t deny it,” he said. He said Iran had fired 925 missiles and drones at Kuwait since the start of the war, and more projectiles at Gulf states and Jordan than at Israel. “This doesn’t fool anyone,” he said.

Al-Shayji said the denial comes down to who was killed and where. “Italian technicians were killed, and not at a US base,” he said.

That undermines Iran’s longstanding argument that it hits only US military targets, he said, an argument he believes had already collapsed because the US has now evacuated 16 bases in the region.

“The justification Iran has always used, ‘we don’t target countries, we target US military bases’, no longer exists,” he said.

Seloom offered two possible explanations. “Either it did not order it, or it cannot afford to own it,” he said.

He noted that Iran’s army openly claimed a strike on Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem airbase last week. “This one hit a Kuwaiti site and killed European civilians, which risks turning Europe and the Gulf hosts against it,” he said.

Kuwaiti officials who spoke to Al Jazeera’s Kuwait bureau on condition of anonymity noted that Iran had not sought a joint investigation after earlier deadly attacks on Kuwait, including the drone strike on the airport.

Some Kuwaiti analysts said the denial appeared to be prompted by the victims’ nationality rather than the attack itself, and Al Jazeera’s bureau chief, Saad al-Saidi, said the Iranian statements had caused resentment in Kuwait.

Von Schirach linked the denial to the pressure Iran is under at home. “All the media reports say the economic situation in Iran is extremely bad,” he said, pointing to protests over the rising cost of living.

“I’m not saying the regime will fall, but it is feeling the heat of pressure from the street,” he said. “Iran is in a very difficult position.”

Not in a combat role, according to Seloom. “Europe’s reflex is pressure,” he said.

He pointed to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who called for more pressure on Tehran, and to Rome, which lodged a complaint with Iran’s embassy while urging caution.

But Seloom said the deaths showed how far Europe is already involved. “The two men were maintaining a Gulf air defence system, so Europe is already in this war as a supplier, and its people are now exposed,” he said.

“Expect sanctions and more defensive support for the Gulf, not European strikes.”

What does this mean for diplomatic efforts to end the war?

The Italian deaths come at a sensitive moment. US President Donald Trump has said he will not consider returning to military action until early next year. That leaves mediators with a few weeks to find terms Washington will accept, chiefly a tangible Iranian concession on its nuclear programme.

Iran has so far stated that it will not discuss its nuclear programme until seven conditions, including the lifting of sanctions and a guaranteed end to US strikes, are met.

Seloom said the drone attack on Kuwait “narrows the track without closing it”. The indirect channel was still running on the day of the strike, he said, with proposals moving through Qatar and Pakistan, according to Araghchi’s own account.

But talks have already stalled and the public position of Qatar, one of the main mediators, is that continued attacks on Kuwait put diplomacy at risk, Seloom said.

He added that the strike strengthens the case for military force, just as the option of targeting Iran’s leadership is being discussed in Washington, according to NBC News. “Washington’s reaction matters more than Kuwait’s,” he said.

Al-Shayji said that whoever is responsible for the drone strikes on Kuwait, Iran’s attacks on Gulf states generally risk lasting damage. “Iran needs to understand that taking revenge on America this way creates enmity with a whole generation” in the Gulf, he said. He added that Kuwait is documenting every Iranian attack and will likely seek compensation.

Ahmadian said confidence building has to go both ways. “Iran didn’t start the war,” he said. “Both sides need to talk about reality, not deny it.”

articles.summary: Turkey pot pie and a turkey potato hash lead a slew of creative Thanksgiving leftovers recipes, from hearty turkey soup to crispy croquettes.
articles.body: With the fridge bursting with leftovers from the big Thanksgiving feast, it's easy to get overwhelmed by the task of using up all that extra food. There's nothing wrong with reheating a plate full of turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, mashed potatoes and other Thanksgiving classics, of course. But for those who want to get creative in the kitchen and keep their palates guessing, there are plenty of ways to liven up leftovers. FOUR FOODS YOU SHOULD NEVER STORE IN THE FREEZER AND WHERE TO KEEP THEM INSTEAD The following chef-created recipes and meal ideas breathe new life into Thanksgiving food in the days that follow the holiday — from a turkey pot pie with a unique topping to a memorable turkey tikka masala. Check these out. Turkey stock and hearty turkey soup Jessica Randhawa of the Forked Spoon in California serves up a comforting turkey soup that's kid-approved. "Made with hearty vegetables, leftover Thanksgiving turkey and pearled barley, my turkey soup recipe is one of my son's favorite leftover Thanksgiving meals, as he is a big fan of hearty and meaty soups," she told Fox News Digital. Making turkey stock is a great way to use all the bones and giblets that get left behind when the bird goes in the oven, Randhawa noted. INA GARTEN SAYS A THANKSGIVING PIE SHORTCUT MAKES HER DESSERT 'ACTUALLY BETTER' Lanie Smith of the Vintage Cook in Kansas also opts for soup after Thanksgiving. "My favorite way to use leftover turkey is by making a broth-forward turkey soup for the freezer," she told Fox News Digital. Smith makes a big pot of her turkey soup recipe and portions it out into individual freezer cups to reheat at a later date. "The best part is pulling it out of the freezer a month or two from now when it's cold outside or one of us is feeling under the weather," she said. "There's nothing better than having a gentle cup of soup to heat up and ready-to-go when you really need it." articles.title: Government to limit costly legal claims aimed at silencing whistleblowers
articles.summary: An MP cited former Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed as someone who used legal action to suppress his "appalling abuse".
articles.body:
The government has pledged to change the law to stop abuse victims, whistleblowers and journalists being silenced by spurious legal actions or threats.

Strategic litigation against public participation, known as Slapps, are often brought by wealthy individuals or companies to stifle scrutiny and suppress matters of public interest.

Existing protections only apply to Slapps linked to economic crime, but the government is now supporting a bill tabled by Conservative MP Sir John Whittingdale to extend protections to all forms of public interest reporting.

Labour's Courts Minister Sarah Sackman said the "justice system should never be a weapon of intimidation".

Speaking in the House of Commons, Sackman said: "The government, working with [Sir John], is determined to stop the wealthy, the powerful using the threat of costly legal proceedings to silence people.

"We are pleased to support the bill and to help ensure that those who expose wrongdoing hold the powerful to account and those who speak out in the public interest are protected."

Opening the debate on his bill, Sir John cited ex-Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed as someone who used legal action to suppress his "appalling abuse of young female employees".

The MP for Maldon said: "That resulted in 27 years in which the information was never publicised."

Hundreds of women have accused Al Fayed of rape, sexual assault and trafficking, after a BBC documentary first publicly detailed the allegations in 2024.

Conservative MP Alicia Kearns said Al Fayed, who died in 2023 aged 94, "turned a culture of abuse and silence into the norm" for women working at Harrods.

The luxury store has previously said it "apologises unreservedly for the sexual abuse inflicted upon survivors by Fayed", and set up a compensation scheme for his victims.

Another example raised by Sir John was journalist Catherine Belton, the author of Putin's People, who faced five legal claims brought by Russian oligarchs and firms.

Sir John also referenced Eliot Higgins, the founder of investigative website Bellingcat, telling MPs he was sued by Yevgeny Prigozhin in 2021 for his tweets suggesting the Russian mercenary leader was associated with the Wagner Group.

He said: "Prigozhin was already sanctioned in this country because of his association yet nevertheless that case was allowed to proceed."

Measures in Sir John's bill include allowing judges to dismiss abusive claims before they go to trial and to protect defendants from exorbitant legal costs.

The UK Anti-Slaap Coalition said last week it "strongly" supports the bill making progress in Parliament although it voiced concerns over its current wording.

It noted there is an "almost impossibly high threshold" to make use of the early dismissal mechanism and offered to work with Sir John and others to refine the bill.

The National Union of Journalists voiced similar concerns, adding the protections must be "truly accessible and robust".

Sir John acknowledged there are concerns over "hurdles" in the proposed legislation which "could act as a deterrent", adding he expects further talks with the minister.

The Strategic Litigation Against Public Participation (No.2) Bill was debated in the House of Commons on Friday and was given an unopposed second reading, which means MPs endorsed the main principles of it.

It will undergo further scrutiny in the Commons at a later date. It will need to be approved by MPs and peers in the House of Lords to become law.

articles.title: Rare turtles found inside baggage at Amsterdam airport
articles.summary: The endangered reptiles were bound with duct tape to prevent them moving, officials say.
articles.body:
Twenty-six "very rare" turtles have been seized from a traveller's checked baggage at Amsterdam's Schiphol airport, a Dutch government agency has said.

The Netherlands Food and Consumer Product Safety Authority (NVWA) said a man flying from Mexico to Hong Kong via the airport was arrested on Saturday after the Vallarta mud turtles were found by customs officers.

The endangered species, thought to be the smallest freshwater turtles in the world with a maximum length of about 10cm (4in), were wrapped in duct tape to prevent them from moving.

The NVWA said they were "presumably stolen" from the wild in their native Mexico.

It said most of the turtles were found in a box with a toy car, while the others were in a closed sock inside a suitcase.

The arrested man remains in custody and an investigation is under way.

Meanwhile, the turtles are receiving care at a "specialised sanctuary", the NVWA said.

In 2025, the US NGO Turtle Island estimated that no more than 300 Vallarta mud turtles existed in the wild.

They are listed as critically endangered on a list published by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.

According to environmental news outlet Mongabay, a Vallarta mud turtle can sell for $10,000 (£7,500) or more on the black market in Asia.

Other cases of live turtles being smuggled to Hong Kong have been reported this year.

In October, customs authorities in Hong Kong were reported to have seized eight turtles that were thought to be endangered. The reptiles had an estimated market value of about $54,000.

Three months prior, Hong Kong customs detected two separate smuggling cases . Some 42 live turtles, with a total estimated market value of $210,000 were seized.

articles.title: Met Police risks losing skills through AI use, report warns
articles.summary: Newly trained officers may never learn key policing skills if they rely on AI, a report warns.
articles.body:
Inexperienced police officers should be made to do their own legwork to solve crimes instead of using AI, according to a report into the use of the technology.

Investigators may never develop crucial crime-fighting skills without manually sifting through evidence and learning about criminals' behaviour, London Assembly member Marina Ahmad's report warned.

Ahmad, deputy chair of the London Assembly's Police and Crime Committee, said the Metropolitan Police operated under its own rules on the use of AI, and called for its use to be regulated.

The Home Office said police forces were "operationally independent" but that any use of AI in policing had to be "lawful and transparent".

In Policing London in the Age of AI , Ahmad said: "Officers become experts, in part, by doing much of the work that AI is now lifting off of them, spending hours trawling through evidence, learning the language of drug dealing, or reading patterns of offender behaviour.

"If AI absorbs those tasks, newer officers may never develop the underlying skill, which poses a risk to their ability to scrutinise the answers an AI tool gives them in future."

Ahmad added: "Training should keep newer officers doing some of this work by hand, so they build the judgement they need to spot when a tool gets it wrong."

The Home Office said outputs from AI should always be subject to human oversight, with officers having to verify results to correct inaccuracies or biases.

It said the government was supporting the police in adopting AI with £115m over the next three years, aimed at freeing up 6 million hours a year for redeployment.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "AI can be a powerful tool to support policing, helping speed up investigations and freeing up officers' time so they can focus on frontline work.

"Any use of these technologies by the police must be lawful and transparent, with robust governance in place."

Writing more broadly about the use of AI in policing, Ahmad said the Met was "the most frequent user of the most debated tools".

It was recently at the centre of a debate over use of Palantir products , with the Metropolitan Police Federation, which represents rank-and-file officers, objecting to the use of the company's technology to monitor the workforce.

In recent years, the force has come in for criticism over its use of live facial recognition (LFR) technology to find wanted criminals in crowds.

Although the new laws around LFR have been proposed , Ahmad is calling for further legislation and an independent regulator to oversee the use of AI by the Met.

She acknowledged the force had "built an impressive and substantial body of internal governance around its use of AI," but added: "A rule that a force writes for itself is one it can revise, widen or relax at its own discretion.

"And beneath all of it lies the absence of any legislation specifically governing police use of AI."

articles.title: Ilia Malinin destroza el récord del mundo del programa corto
articles.standfirst: El patinador estadounidense recibe 114,81 puntos en el NHK Trophy de Tokio y bate la plusmarca mundial de Nathan Chen
articles.summary: El patinador estadounidense recibe 114,81 puntos en el NHK Trophy de Tokio y bate la plusmarca mundial de Nathan Chen
articles.body: Ilia Malinin añade un nuevo hito a su palmarés. El patinador estadounidense estableció un nuevo récord del mundo en el programa corto. A sus 21 años recibió 114,81 puntos como valoración de su ejercicio en el Grand Prix NHK Trophy de Tokio (Japón). Pulverizó la anterior plusmarca de 113,97 en posesión de Nathan Chen desde los Juegos Olímpicos de Pekín en 2022. Malinin ganó su tercer Mundial con la que hasta ahora era su mejor marca en el programa corto (111,29). Con ese oro se desquitó del fiasco de los Juegos de Milán-Cortina, en los que dos caídas en el programa libre le dejaron fuera del podio (acabó octavo) cuando partía como el gran favorito. En Japón, con la música de la 'Cantata Memoria-Lament for the Valley', de Karl Jenkins, Malinin ejecutó a la perfección un cuádruple, un triple axel y un cuádruple lutz con triple toe y una combinación de cuádruple lutz y triple toe loop. Un ejercicio que le dio el récord del mundo del programa corto que suma al que ya poseía del libre con 238,24. Ilia, el 'dios de los cuádruples', eligió esta música y este programa corto de cara a esta nueva temporada como homenaje a las víctimas del accidente de un avión en las aguas del río Potomac (Washington D.C.) en el que murieron 67 personas, entre ellas varios jóvenes patinadores estadounidenses actuales, así como otros rusos ya retirados y ahora entrenadores. Originalmente, Jenkins estrenó la Cantata Memoria en 2016 en un concierto conmemorativo del 50 aniversario del desastre minero de Aberfan de 1966. "Se ha convertido en una pieza musical universal para la tragedia o los acontecimientos trágicos. Quería mostrar esta nueva faceta mía, este lado vulnerable, emotivo y sensible, para ver si tal vez eso puede cambiar lo que la gente piensa de mí", explicó Malinin cuando presentó su nuevo programa. Malinin participa en su segunda prueba del Grand Prix de la temporada. Ya ganó el Skate America este mes. De momento, lidera el NHK Trophy de Tokio con esos 114,81 puntos por delante del japonés Shun Sato, con 96,78 puntos, y el francés Kevin Aymoz, con 94,15.

articles.title: Pakistan to host Saudi, Turkiye defence meet as Houthi attacks raise regional tensions
articles.summary: Pakistan is set to host senior defence and foreign affairs officials from Saudi Arabia and Turkiye for a two-day meeting in Islamabad, with the escalating
articles.body: Pakistan is set to host senior defence and foreign affairs officials from Saudi Arabia and Turkiye for a two-day meeting in Islamabad, with the escalating conflict between Riyadh and Yemen's Houthi rebels expected to feature prominently in discussions.The meeting comes amid a fresh round of hostilities between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis, who have repeatedly targeted the Gulf kingdom with attacks on strategic infrastructure, including oil facilities and airports.The gathering will take place under the trilateral Makkah Defence Alliance, a security pact signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye in August. The agreement provides for collective deterrence, meaning an armed attack on any one of the three countries would be treated as an attack on all three.The third session of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee (SPDC), the alliance's top decision-making body, will begin on Friday, Dawn newspaper reported.Authorities have declared a public holiday in Islamabad on Friday and imposed special movement restrictions in the capital and neighbouring Rawalpindi ahead of the high-level meeting.Defence minister Khawaja Asif confirmed that the foreign and defence ministers of all three countries would participate in the meeting, describing it as "very important"."The continuous turmoil south of Saudi Arabia will obviously be on the agenda," Dawn quoted Asif as saying."Any threat to Saudi Arabia is a threat to Pakistan and Turkiye according to the pact, which is absolutely clear," he said.Saudi-Houthi conflict likely to dominate talksSaudi Arabia has faced repeated attacks by Yemen's Houthi militia, which has targeted key infrastructure, including oil installations and airports.On Tuesday, the Houthis struck a tower in the financial district of the Saudi capital, damaging the building and injuring 11 people. The injured included two Indian and three Nepalese nationals.Saudi Arabia retaliated on Thursday by carrying out strikes in western and southwestern Yemen.The latest developments come as Islamabad seeks to maintain diplomatic engagement with other regional powers. A day before the scheduled meeting, Pakistan's deputy prime minister and foreign minister Ishaq Dar spoke with his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi over the phone.The two leaders discussed the broader regional situation and efforts to promote peace and security.Alliance moves towards implementing defence pactThe upcoming meeting follows an emergency session of the SPDC held in Riyadh on October 5, during which Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye agreed to begin implementing their collective defence commitments.The three countries decided to take necessary steps to provide the military forces and capabilities agreed under the pact and ensure their swift deployment in Saudi Arabia.Pakistan has also reiterated its readiness to support the kingdom amid rising regional tensions.Earlier this month, Pakistan Army spokesperson Lt Gen Ahmed Sharif Chaudhry said Islamabad was prepared to take "all necessary defensive measures" to protect Saudi Arabia.In an interview with a Saudi newspaper, Chaudhry described Pakistan's commitment to the kingdom's security, sovereignty and territorial integrity as "absolute and non-negotiable".He said Pakistani troops were already deployed in Saudi Arabia, where they primarily provide defensive support and participate in joint military exercises and manoeuvres.However, he did not disclose details about the number of troops stationed in the kingdom or the specific nature of their deployment.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'We have no interest in hearing from Huw Edwards', Downing Street says
articles.summary: There has been a backlash against new interviews with the disgraced former BBC News presenter.
articles.body:
The prime minister's spokesperson has said broadcasters must "act responsibly" and that "we have no interest in hearing" what Huw Edwards has to say, following a backlash against new interviews with the disgraced former BBC News presenter.

Edwards, who was convicted in 2024 for making indecent images of children, has been interviewed for a Channel 4 documentary plus a podcast by the Observer and Tortoise Media.

"Our thoughts first and foremost will be with the victims of child sexual abuse and exploitation. We have no interest in hearing what he has to say," a Downing Street spokesperson said.

"There are extremely serious crimes and anyone convicted of them must face the consequences of their actions."

The No 10 spokesperson added that broadcasters "are expected to act responsibly and have appropriate regards to their audiences when making decisions".

Pressed on whether the prime minister believed Channel 4 had not acted responsibly, they said: "Channel 4 is editorially independent and decisions about individual programmes and contributors are a matter for them."

During the court case, Edwards admitted three counts of making indecent images of children. That involved having 41 images and videos, which were sent to him on WhatsApp – including some showing a victim aged between seven and nine.

Earlier, Environment Minister Emma Hardy said the plan by Channel 4 made her feel "sick", telling LBC it was giving a platform to "someone who is on the Sex Offenders Register".

"That platform doesn't exist for his child victims, does it?... It's not something I could support, and it's definitely not something I'd be watching."

Channel 4 has defended the programme, telling the BBC a "highly experienced director", Patrick Forbes, held Edwards to account with "no questions off limits, revealing his account of what led to his offending and very public downfall".

Conservative MP Dame Caroline Dinenage, chair of the House of Commons culture and media select committee, said the media outlets should "not just act as a platform" for Edwards to have a voice.

Any programme featuring him "needs to properly challenge his past actions" she said, along with raising "still unanswered questions" about whether Edwards will return more than £200,000 he was paid by the BBC , after he was first arrested.

The documentary and podcast will both be released on Tuesday, with some material expected to be published by the Observer on Sunday.

The interviews have also been criticised by three people who previously spoke to BBC News about allegations of Edwards' inappropriate behaviour.

One, who accused him in 2023 of sending them threatening messages, said it was "incredibly bizarre that anyone, big names like Channel Four, are platforming him when he's a convicted sex offender".

The person, who is anonymous and not connected to the criminal case, told BBC News on Thursday Edwards was "clearly trying to do a bit of damage repair" and they were "annoyed that he's being able to air these opinions".

Another person, who said Edwards sent them suggestive and "pushy" messages when they were working at the BBC, and was also not involved in the court case, said: "I'm pretty disgusted they are giving him the air time."

Additionally, a former junior BBC employee, who previously told BBC Newsnight's Victoria Derbyshire they had received inappropriate messages from Edwards, said "it seems a strange and irresponsible decision to give a platform to tell his story after the crimes he has been found guilty of.

"I hope that consideration has been given to his victims."

Duncan Craig, head of We Are Survivors, which supports male survivors of sexual abuse and rape, said it felt like the media companies were "not thinking about the victims in this particular case".

And it is the wrong time to release these programmes, coming during "a reckoning moment" for abuse in the media, he added.

"[It is] in fact giving somebody a platform that, in some way, shape or form, gives them the ability to nail themselves to the cross. That is not OK."

He added he does "fundamentally believe in rehabilitation" but that "this doesn't feel like it."

In a promotional clip released by the Observer, interviewer Ceri Thomas is seen saying he was "just deeply curious about how it was that a man of such prominence had got himself into this unbelievable, terrible fix".

"An 'unbelievable terrible fix' isn't somebody sat actively downloading 41 images of child sexual abuse, of which a number of them were at grade A level of of boys aged seven to nine being sexually abused," he said.

BBC broadcaster Nicky Campbell added his voice, saying: "I'm rather more concerned for the children in the photographs. What of their lives?"

The Observer, which is owned by Tortoise Media, has been asked for a response to the criticism.

Meanwhile, journalist Sangita Myska posted : "The rehabilitation [of] Huw Edwards' reputation via a 'personal journey' documentary is contemptible. He's a sex offender. What the hell is Channel 4 thinking?"

Fellow broadcaster Richard Bacon responded : "Why is that rehabilitation? It's a documentary. There are lots of them about lots of different people. About lots of different types of people."

articles.title: Canada's top court largely upholds Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
articles.summary: The law faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.
articles.body:
Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.

The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.

Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.

The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.

Reacting to the ruling on CBC, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would study its implications, adding it was important for all legislatures "to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority."

The Supreme Court was asked to weigh in on a number of questions, including on the constitutionality of Bill 21, whether Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause was appropriate, and whether there are limits to its use.

On Friday, the top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, but ruled that the law infringes on democratic rights by banning Quebec's elected officials from wearing a face covering for religious reasons.

The court also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.

While the majority of the seven justices found that Quebec's law is largely valid, some dissented to parts of the decision.

Justices Andromache Karakatsanis, Michelle O'Bonsawin and Nicholas Kasirer wrote that the notwithstanding clause "cannot be used to authorize laws that are incompatible with the fundamental character of Canada as a free and democratic country".

Specifically, they said they believe the law infringes on the charter's guarantee to freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.

What to know about the Supreme Court decision on Quebec's secularism bill

Civil liberty groups in Quebec have criticised Bill 21, saying it disproportionately affects Muslim women who wear the hijab, arguing that it has excluded them from key areas of public life in the province.

Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, called the law "discriminatory" and criticised the court's decision.

"Entire categories of people are now barred from entire sectors of employment, not because of what they have done, but because of who they are," he said.

The chair of the English Montreal School Board, one of the main groups challenging the law, said the board was "obviously very disappointed" with the ruling.

"It wasn't the result we were looking for," Ortona told reporters. "But we do take solace from a lot of the declarations that were made by the court."

Quebec has argued that the law is necessary to uphold the province's state secularism - or laïcité - as a core component of its identity.

Earlier this year, the province passed another bill expanding its secularism rules to subsidised daycares and post-secondary institutions. It also restricted public prayer with fines for non-compliance.

The leader of the Bloc Québécois, a federal party that advocates for Quebec sovereignty, said Friday's ruling upheld the province's right to protect its values.

"We are now more than ever in a position to move forward with the preservation of the very elements that profoundly define the distinct nature of Quebec society," Yves-François Blanchet told reporters in French.

articles.title: Ukraine is bowed but still unbroken as freezing weather sets in
articles.summary: Ukraine settles in for another devastating winter as the questions persists: how will it all end?
articles.body:
Something weird happens when you reach Kyiv after the eight-hour drive from the Polish border: the clock on your mobile phone goes to midnight. It's not really for phones - it seems to be part of a wider strategy to disorient the missiles and drones the Russians are sending over.

Aside from little things like that, though, Kyiv seems fairly normal at first sight. You become well aware there's a war on when sirens begin to wail and people check their phones for the notifications which tell them there's a red alert and missiles are on their way. You can even buy gadgets that show you which direction the drones are coming from, and what type they are.

The drones and ballistic missiles have been hitting in sizeable numbers over the last couple of weeks. On the morning of Monday 16 November, the battle of the bridges began. Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge which links Russia to illegally occupied Crimea. Then it launched a bigger wave of missiles and drones, damaging the central road-bridge arch. A few hours later, presumably in revenge, Russia fired seven ballistic missiles at Kyiv, disabling two of the nine bridges that cross the River Dnipro.

The war has dragged on for more than four and a half years, killing what some estimate could be 100,000 Ukrainian troops and 18,000 Ukrainian civilians, according to the United Nations, and probably more. Its infrastructure, too, has been battered, as well as its morale. While temperatures drop to freezing at night, and with Ukrainians regularly suffering from no light, heat or water thanks to Russian strikes, can the country survive another difficult winter under bombardment? And what would a peace deal, if one could be struck, look like?

Kyiv is mostly dark at night, thanks to Russia's campaign of targeting Ukraine's electricity generating capability. In the blackness last week, the air raid sirens started wailing across the city, and our hotel's warning announcements came over the loudspeakers. Within a few minutes, we heard the first explosions. I jumped out of bed and stared out of the window into the darkness. After a few seconds two more missiles landed, lighting up the entire sky momentarily in a blaze of white and red. They were uncomfortably close.

Many people prefer to go to the shelters when there's a red alert. Others just stay in bed and hope the law of averages will protect them. It usually does. During one of the heaviest attacks last week, the number of fatalities was in single figures.

I went to the shelter in our hotel one night. The clearly audible thumps and crashes above ground, the permanent lighting, the snores and grunts of other people, and the attentions of the little biting flies that seem to thrive in the warm, crowded shelters made sleep hard.

To the people who live here in Kyiv, it's frightening, certainly, if a drone or a missile hits close by, but enraging too. Over the years I've been in several cities that were being bombed by high-tech weaponry and the reaction always seems the same, whether it's Lebanon, Iraq, Serbia, or Ukraine: a combination of weariness and fury. In Kyiv the attacks come by night and day, making normal life almost impossible. An uninterrupted night's sleep is a rarity. The morning after the bridges were hit, people in the streets looked tired and worn.

Yet although they long for it to stop, there's no sign they want Ukraine to surrender. On the contrary, just about everyone I spoke to felt they had to keep fighting. That's borne out by an opinion poll last month by the KIIS organisation, a Ukrainian market research company, which found that 62% of people were prepared to put up with the war for as long as it took. Of those polled, 79% believed that Ukraine would win the war in the long run, and only 7% thought Russia would win. These aren't the reactions of a country which is being beaten to its knees.

I don't have any doubt that Ukraine can survive the winter. Food is plentiful, though prices are high. Water is a problem, because the regular attacks on the power grid mean that it can't be pumped with any regularity. Kyiv underwent a large transformation under the Soviets, so there are large numbers of high-rise blocks of flats everywhere. Labouring up and down the stairs when there's no power is daunting, especially when you've got to carry quantities of water home.

We came across a small crowd of people in their 20s who had gathered outside a nightclub for a rave at three in the afternoon, because of the 11pm curfew. "It's a way of getting a bit of respite from everything," said one young woman. "It makes me feel I can put up with everything," said a man.

Do people still support President Volodymyr Zelensky? My team and I met an elderly woman wandering around Independence Square in the centre of Kyiv holding a photo of her son, who was missing on the Eastern front. She blamed Zelensky; if he didn't insist on carrying on the war, she believed, her son would still be alive. It isn't a response most people seem to share. The same polling organisation, KIIS, found that Zelensky's trust ratings hover around 54% to 57% — way below the 90% he was registering in the early days of the war in 2022, but not too bad for a man who's been in power now for more than seven years.

What comes across all the time in Kyiv is an absolute loathing of Russia. Putin reportedly launched his invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 because his intelligence chiefs assured him that Ukrainians longed to rejoin the Motherland.

Russian missiles have hit hospitals, clinics and schools. In many well-attested cases the Russians have used the "double-tap" method — sending in one missile, then waiting till the medics and rescuers gather before sending in another. At least 20,000 Ukrainian children have been abducted and taken to Russia, according to Ukraine's Ministry of Justice. In late March 2022, when the Ukrainians recaptured the satellite town of Bucha, on the outskirts of Kyiv, they found shocking evidence of torture and murder. Ukrainian soldiers call their Russian enemies Orcs, after the sub-human brutes in The Lord of the Rings. A country that has endured this kind of thing doesn't quickly forgive and forget. Russia denies that it targets civilians or civilian infrastructure.

Ukraine has never lost its own identity, even during the Soviet period. Some of Ukraine's culture was absorbed by Russia — "They call borsch [a famously delicious soup made of beetroot] theirs, but they got it from us," a waiter in a café here told me proudly. After the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, Ukraine overwhelmingly voted for independence. The war has brought a fierce renewal of this desire to be completely separated from Russia.

It's not my usual beat, but my team and I went to film on the set of MasterChef Ukraine, currently one of the country's favourite television programmes. The studio was borrowed; the original one had been bombed. The executive producer had his phone in his hand the whole time, and was constantly glancing at it. The moment a red alert showed, it was his duty to shepherd everyone off the set to a nearby shelter. "People see our cuisine as a way of expressing their national identity," he said. It's one of the reasons the programme is so popular.

There are other ways in which people express their Ukrainian national identity under the bombs. There has been a boom for books being written and published about Ukraine and Ukrainian identity. Ukrainian and Russian are close as languages, though vocabulary and pronunciation differ. Nowadays the differences are emphasised. "Woe betide a writer who uses Russian spellings," a Ukrainian novelist told me.

The war will end at some point; wars always do. But there has to be a clear winner before anyone backs down, and a lasting peace can be negotiated. US President Donald Trump and his advisers, people like Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, with their business backgrounds, have approached the situation as though it's a form of mergers and acquisitions: make a deal attractive enough, and the other side will accept it.

So, last week, Washington was rumoured to be offering a very Trumpian deal, that Ukraine should accept the loss of the land in the east which the Russians now control, and in return it was rumoured it could join Nato. It was a non-starter, because Russia would never accept it. The sweetener, in this US plan, was that the West's sanctions against Russia would be lifted, and both sides would benefit from unrestricted trading once again.

But neither side sees this as being about trade and profit. For Russia, it's about the dangers of being humiliated if it doesn't win. President Vladimir Putin has made it his personal war. By illegally taking Crimea from Ukraine in 2014, he made himself very popular in Russia. If he doesn't win this second stage of a 12-year campaign against Ukraine, the consequences for him personally could be disastrous. He's already had to face down one attempt against his rule: his former associate Yevgeny Prigozhin's march on Moscow in June 2023. In a much-quoted remark, reported last August, Putin is said to have confided to his associates that if he didn't win the war "they'll hang me". My sense is he's not concerned about trade with the West and the profit that will bring, so much as about his personal survival.

Similarly, Ukrainians aren't interested in the precise details that have leaked out of the various negotiations between the Americans and Russians. Their contempt for the US is immense; "they just failed us," said one Ukrainian I spoke to.

And they don't believe Russia will stick to any future peace agreement anyway. "They signed a treaty to accept our borders, and Putin broke it," a young man told me as he sat hunched over his laptop in a bookshop. "The only solution is to defeat them."

Other people talked about the need to get huge reparations from Russia for the terrible destruction it has visited on their country. According to one estimate, reconstruction and recovery will cost more than $500bn (£383bn), an unthinkably huge amount for a country whose GDP was $200bn before the war. President Trump and his advisers don't seem to have addressed any of these issues in their negotiations.

Here in Kyiv, peace doesn't seem at all close. Russia's efforts to make life intolerable for Ukraine's citizens are certainly having a major effect. The war is often frightening for ordinary people, and it can be appallingly destructive of property and lives. But short of hugely escalating by attacking Ukraine with nuclear weapons, which is something China and the US are both thought to have warned him not to do, Putin can't seem to strike the knock-out blow against Ukraine that he needs.

At present it seems to people in Ukraine that the war will never come to an end. Yet it will, at some point: and then the crucial requirement will be to work out ways to stop Russia coming back for another round. One way would be if Ukraine joins Nato, but that's something Russia would only accept if it had been comprehensively defeated. Ukrainians might think that can happen, but most Western onlookers are more sceptical.

The daily and nightly sirens, the explosions of missiles and drones, the shortages and the fear and the darkness are all terrible. But they aren't enough to destroy Ukraine's will to continue fighting.

articles.title: Reform's Joe Martin threatens legal challenge after being banned from speaking in Senedd
articles.summary: Joe Martin has been told he must apologise for referring to the "replacement" of white people.
articles.body:
A Reform UK politician banned from speaking in the Senedd after referring to the "replacement" of white people in the UK says he will seek legal action to overturn the decision.

Joe Martin said elected representatives should be able to "speak up for the people who elected them" and raise "difficult subjects".

The Free Speech Union (FSU) campaign group said Huw Irranca-Davies' ruling breached European law, and has sent a pre-action letter challenging it.

The Senedd Commission, which runs the parliament, declined to comment.

On Thursday night, Martin, who represents the Caerdydd Penarth constituency, called the ruling an "unprecedented attack on free speech".

Martin accused what he called a "uniparty" in Cardiff Bay of trying to silence Reform and protect a "cosy consensus".

"That is why I have taken legal action to defend the right to free speech in Wales," he said.

"Every elected representative should have the right to speak up for the people who elected them, without being silenced simply for raising difficult subjects."

FSU said it had sent a pre-action letter to the Senedd Commission, calling for the decision to be reversed, and said it argued that Irranca-Davies "misused his powers".

It also said the decision to prevent Martin from speaking and an order for him to apologise breached Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights , which is the right to freedom of expression.

The ban was handed to Martin earlier this month , after he had asked a minister for a "statement from your government on the demographic replacement of white British people taking place" in the UK.

"Mass immigration and differing birth rates mean that, in just 37 years' time, in 2063, we will be a minority in our own country," he said.

Irranca-Davies had described Martin's words as "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive", but stressed that members could "raise legitimate policy matters" on immigration.

Martin's focus "on race and ethnicity was clearly discriminatory, offensive and detracted from the dignity of the Senedd", Irranca-Davies previously said.

He said Martin would not be called to speak in the Senedd chamber until he had received "clear indication that the member understands the boundaries of acceptable parliamentary conduct and apologises".

In June, Plaid Cymru had accused Martin of dangerous rhetoric for claiming attacks from Sudanese asylum seekers were inevitable.

The next day Senedd members walked out during a speech where Martin joked that Welsh students were unable to read and Indian nurses were taking Welsh jobs .

He was later accused by the presiding officer of making offensive remarks in a debate about the Welsh Gender Service .

articles.title: An Arizona couple bought a Phoenix home in 1998 and separated a year later without divorcing; after another woman lived there for 24 years, a November 23 court confirmed ownership passed to the estranged wife
articles.summary: A court ruling confirms the ownership of a Phoenix home belongs to an estranged wife after her husband passed away, despite another woman living there for 24 years. Discover the legal implications of joint tenancy and adverse possession in this complex case.
articles.body: An Arizona woman has retained ownership of a Phoenix home she bought with her husband in 1998, despite moving out a year later and living separately from him for more than two decades. The Arizona Court of Appeals has upheld her ownership rights after rejecting a claim brought by another woman who lived in the property with her estranged husband for 24 years.The ruling, filed on Monday, confirmed Rita Mack's ownership of the house following the death of her husband, Troy Torrence, in September 2024. The couple had separated in 1999 but never divorced, and their property remained jointly owned under an arrangement that transferred the surviving owner's share upon the other's death.Dimica Hicks, who moved into the house with Torrence in 2000, challenged Mack's ownership and sought reimbursement for expenses she claimed to have paid towards the property. However, the appeals court found no grounds to overturn the lower court's decision in Mack's favour.Couple separated a year after buying the Phoenix propertyMack and Torrence purchased the Amberlea Property in Phoenix in 1998 as joint tenants with the right of survivorship. Under this arrangement, the surviving joint tenant automatically receives the deceased owner's interest.The following year, Mack moved out after separating from Torrence. However, the couple's marriage was never dissolved, and neither of them took steps to end the joint tenancy or transfer their ownership interest.Hicks moved into the property in 2000 and remained there until Torrence died in September 2024. She was subsequently appointed the personal representative of his estate.In December 2024, Hicks filed a lawsuit seeking ownership of the house through adverse possession. She also argued that her contributions towards mortgage payments, maintenance, property taxes, insurance and utilities entitled her to financial compensation.Mack disputed the claims, maintaining that she had become the sole owner following Torrence's death under the original joint ownership arrangement.Woman's 24-year stay did not establish ownership rightsThe Maricopa County Superior Court granted Mack summary judgment on the ownership and constructive trust claims, finding that Hicks had not established adverse possession.Under Arizona law, a person seeking ownership through adverse possession must demonstrate that their occupation was open, notorious, continuous, exclusive and hostile to the legal owner's rights.The court found that Hicks had lived in the house with Torrence's permission. This meant her occupation did not establish hostile possession or show that she had excluded the legal owners from their rights.The Arizona Court of Appeals agreed, noting that one joint tenant occupying an entire property does not automatically terminate the joint tenancy. It also found no evidence that the original ownership arrangement had been dissolved or that Hicks had exercised exclusive possession.The appeals court concluded that Mack acquired Torrence's share through the right of survivorship after his death, making her the property's sole owner.Appeals court rejects reimbursement claim and upholds rulingHicks also sought compensation for mortgage payments and improvements she said she had made to the property. However, the lower court rejected her unjust enrichment claim after a bench trial in November 2025.The court found that some mortgage payments had come from Torrence's employment income or Social Security disability benefits. It also noted that Hicks had not contributed consistently towards the mortgage and had received value from her payments by living in the house for several years.Hicks challenged the outcome, arguing that she had been denied an opportunity to cross-examine Mack and that the courts had failed to properly consider the evidence.The appeals court rejected these arguments, noting that Hicks had neither listed Mack as a witness nor subpoenaed her for the trial. It also found that she had not raised an objection during the proceedings.In its Monday decision, a three-judge panel of the Arizona Court of Appeals affirmed the lower court's judgment, leaving Mack as the sole owner of the Phoenix property.You use AI every day. articles.title: Brazil pushes back on Emmanuel Macron calling its meat 'doped'
articles.summary: France's president made the comment while speaking to French farming representatives, months after the EU banned Brazil beef and poultry products.
articles.body:
Brazil says it "regrets" a statement by French President Emmanuel Macron who called Brazilian meat "doped".

France's leader made the comment while meeting representatives of farming unions on Wednesday, during which he celebrated EU restrictions on imports of Brazilian meat and poultry which took effect in September.

In its statement, the Brazilian government said Macron's statements "spread misinformation and contradict the widely available technical and scientific evidence on animal protein production in Brazil".

Macron's comments come as part of a trade row between the EU and Mercosur - the South American trade bloc. The EU banned Brazilian meat, poultry and other animal products owing to the use of antimicrobials in farming.

In its defence, Brazil said it had supplied animal protein to the EU for decades and that it exported meat to 177 markets. It added the country had a rigorous sanitary control system, corroborated by a recent European audit, and observed stringent environmental requirements.

Macron, in his opening remarks in the meeting with the agricultural sector representatives at Élysée Palace, said he was "proud of the fight we led" against Mercosur.

"And the 'doped' meat, if I may put it that way, or rather meat from Mercosur countries, especially Brazil, that was arriving in our ports and therefore entering our markets without complying with our rules, was ultimately banned," he said.

Brazil said it was concerned about the "clearly political nature" of recent EU restrictions, and urged France to reconsider its position "in light of scientific evidence".

Affirming its partnership with France was important, the country emphasised that "in the face of protectionist pressures, the best interests of the bilateral relationship must prevail, always guided by mutual respect and reciprocity".

Brazil is a massive exporter of meat, especially beef - some $1.84bn (£1.4bn) of which went to EU markets alone in 2025, according to Brazil's agricultural ministry.

articles.title: Inside Anmer Hall, where Prince William and Kate Middleton raised their family, spent Covid lockdown, Catherine recovered from cancer treatment, before two masked men broke in

articles.body: Anmer Hall, the 10-bedroom Georgian country residence of Prince William and Kate Middleton, is located in the village of Anmer in Norfolk, northeastern England. Situated within the sprawling Sandringham Estate, the historic property serves as a private country retreat for the Prince and Princess of Wales and their three children.The secluded residence recently came into the spotlight after two masked men reportedly broke into the property on Monday. Local police arrested two men on suspicion of burglary and trespass, according to The Times. Police said the estate was unoccupied at the time of the incident, and the suspects remain in custody.The reported break-in has drawn attention to the property, which holds considerable personal significance for William and Kate. It was also where Catherine recuperated following surgery and cancer treatment in 2024. Here's a closer look at where Anmer Hall is, its royal history and the interiors of the family's country retreat.Where is Anmer Hall located?Anmer Hall is situated in the quaint village of Anmer in Norfolk, a coastal county in northeastern England, approximately a three-hour drive from London. The 10-bedroom Georgian house, built in 1802, is part of the 20,000-acre Sandringham Estate, which has been associated with the British royal family since 1862.The estate is also home to Sandringham House, the country residence of King Charles III and Queen Camilla, where the royal family traditionally celebrates Christmas. Anmer Hall is around a five-minute drive from the main residence.Unlike Sandringham House, which welcomes visitors for tours, Anmer Hall remains a private family residence.What is Anmer Hall and what is its history?Anmer Hall is a two-storey Georgian country house with a distinctive red-and-brown brick facade, 13 bays and dormer windows. Its history dates back several centuries, when it served as the seat of the Coldham family.Prince Albert Edward, later King Edward VII, purchased the property in 1896 and made it part of the Sandringham Estate. The house underwent renovations following the acquisition and was subsequently leased to several members of the British aristocracy.Among its former residents were the Duke and Duchess of Kent, who lived there from 1972 to 1990, and Hugh van Cutsem, a close friend of King Charles III. After van Cutsem's lease expired, the property was rented to timber company owner James Everett.How did Anmer Hall become William and Kate's family home?Anmer Hall became particularly significant to William and Kate following their marriage in 2011. In 2013, reports emerged that the couple were considering the property as their family home.At the time, they were living in a rented farmhouse in Anglesey, Wales, where Prince William worked as a helicopter pilot. The couple were also expecting their first child, Prince George.Former royal correspondent Michael Cole told the BBC that Anmer Hall appeared to be an ideal choice because it was close to the Queen but not too close.Later that year, it was confirmed that William and Kate would move into the property with Prince George. However, the family moved in only in 2015, when Kate was expecting their second child, Princess Charlotte.The house underwent a reported $2 million refurbishment before their arrival. The improvements included a new roof, additional trees for privacy and interior upgrades.In 2017, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle also stayed at Anmer Hall with William and Kate. The property later served as the Wales family's home during the Covid lockdown.Today, William and Kate spend most of their time at Forest Lodge on the grounds of Windsor Castle, but Anmer Hall remains their country escape.Inside Anmer Hall: A look at William and Kate's country homeAs part of the property's refurbishment, the Prince and Princess of Wales enlisted architect Charles Morris to oversee the renovation and interior designer Ben Pentreath to work on the interiors. Pentreath had also redesigned the couple's apartment at Kensington Palace, according to House & Garden.His design philosophy draws inspiration from traditional English interiors of the 18th and 19th centuries, alongside influences from the 1960s and 1970s, with a contemporary approach.The same aesthetic can be seen in glimpses of Anmer Hall shared through the royal couple's social media posts. The interiors feature high ceilings, decorative mouldings, soothing neutral shades, antiques, houseplants and gilt-framed artwork. The dining room is reportedly decorated in a deep green shade.The property also boasts a swimming pool and a tennis court. Anmer Hall even has its own honeybee colony and is said to have a ghost story associated with it.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
