articles.title: In 1976, a Georgia couple buried a letter for their young sons; 50 years later, it resurfaced with their father’s message, though he had died 24 years earlier
articles.summary: Discover the touching story of a handwritten letter buried in a Georgia time capsule 50 years ago, revealing a father's love and hopes for his sons as the capsule is reopened for the first time since 1976.
articles.body: Handwritten letters have always occupied an irreplaceable spot in the hearts of families. Fifty years ago, a time capsule was buried beneath the sidewalk located outside a Georgia courthouse, preserving a record of everyday life during America’s bicentennial. On June 30, 2026, to kick off Whitfield County’s weeklong celebration of America’s 250th anniversary, hundreds of residents assembled at the Whitfield County Courthouse as the county workers uncovered a time vault that had been sealed since 1976, as per the Dalton Daily Citizen.The capsule contained numerous items, including handwritten letters, newspapers, keepsakes, and other personal mementos, placed there by local families around five decades ago. Originally organized by the Dalton Exchange Club as a part of the nation’s bicentennial celebrations, the project allowed the Whitfield County residents to insert items for $5 per family before the concrete container was buried outside the courthouse at the end of May 1976.Discoveries inside the vault and water damage When Public Works crews did the heavy lifting and pulled back the lid, they discovered trash bags that were filled with envelopes waiting for their owners. However, the decades beneath the surface had done their damage. According to the Chattanooga Times Free Press, resident Todd Looper, whose family contributed to the capsule, shed light on the condition of the items found, noting that everything pulled from the bags was damp and that standing water had collected at the bottom of the vault.Matt Gramling, director of the Bandy Heritage Center, which helped with the opening of the time capsule, stated that some of the discoveries reflected the era in unexpected ways. One of the items that stood out to Gramling was a 1970s carpet. He further revealed that the vault contained an 1881 silver dollar that someone had sealed inside. Even though the carpet had turned musty after years of moisture, most of the capsule’s contents remained legible and intact enough to reveal their history.A handwritten letter for the kids Among the items was a handwritten letter that Looper’s parents, Donna Ivester and Harry Looper, had penned to their two young sons before sealing it away. At the time, Todd was five years old and his brother Brian was one. “My dearest Todd + Brian,” the letter started. “I hope when this is opened your dad + I will still be here on this earth, but if we’re not, I just want to take a few moments to write this note.”The letter looked back on the family memories and expressed hope that the boys would lead purposeful and successful lives. Harry, who passed away in 2002, concluded the message with a simple wish: “Daddy loves you both. You’re fine, boys, and I’m looking forward to my grandchildren.” Todd mentioned that unsealing the envelope stirred up old memories for his mother, who had long forgotten what she had tucked inside all those years ago.Other items found included calendars, newspapers, and letters written to future community leaders. One message, intended for Dalton’s current mayor, Annalee Sams, was scheduled to be read aloud by officials at the July 20, 2026 city council meeting once the paper had dried. Furthermore, officials reported that the unclaimed items would eventually be added to the Bandy Heritage Center’s archives, and conversations had already begun regarding creating a new time capsule, this time housed inside the courthouse rather than buried.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2000, a UK family hid a note under a floorboard; nearly 26 years later, their son saw his late mother's handwriting
articles.summary: A heartfelt message hidden in a floorboard by the Little family in 2000 was discovered in 2026 by an electrician who attended the same school as the writer, leading to a sentimental reunion for their son.
articles.body: A message left behind by a family on an ordinary day at home ended up travelling into the future more than its writers could have anticipated. When an electrician lifted a floorboard in Whickham, Gateshead, in January 2026, he found a glass jar, according to the BBC. Inside it was a handwritten note dated November 2000. The message named two parents, their young children, and the reason they left it behind for whoever found it.For Callum Little, one of the children’s names on the paper, the discovery struck a sentimental chord. It brought back a discovery he had not expected to see again: his late mother’s handwriting.How the note ended up beneath the boardsAccording to the BBC, the note was placed in the house on 25 November 2000, at 6 pm, when the Littles were in the midst of redecorating their house. Wendy and John Little had moved into the property in October 1994, the report noted. While lifting the carpet, they came across a loose floorboard and decided to use the space beneath it to leave a message for any future tenant.It was Wendy who penned the note, setting down the names of the family members under the roof, alongside the tender ages of their children. At the time, Kirsty was seven, and Callum was four. She wrote too of the happenstance that revealed the loose board, alongside the shared whim that made them seal a message inside that space.An electrician’s find and a familiar name The jar remained concealed until Tuesday, 6 January 2026, when electrician Shaun Nesbitt discovered it while rewiring the property, the BBC reported. The house, in Whickham, had previously remained in the Little family. John continued living there until his death in 2024, after which the family home was sold.After finding the jar, Nesbitt decided to look for the people named in the message. He turned to social media and shared photographs of the note, hoping someone would recognise the names and help him trace the family. Instead, the trail looped him back to his own past: he realised he had gone to school with Wendy Little.The handwritten note also gave him clues to establish when the jar had been placed in the first place. Its date, time and list of family members provided the details to identify the people who had left it behind.Nesbitt then added his own note to the original paper. He recorded that it had been found and returned on 6 January 2026, along with names. After that, he lowered the jar back beneath the floorboard for someone else to discover in the future.Keeping the time capsule aliveCallum was 29 years old and living in Derby when he learnt about the discovery after being tagged in Nesbitt’s Facebook post. He had not anticipated seeing the message again nearly 26 years after his family left it in the house. Speaking to the BBC, Callum described his reaction to the post: "I was taken aback by it, but at the same time it put a huge smile on my face just to see my mam's handwriting and the fact that the post was getting so much recognition from people in Whickham."His mother had passed away in 2016, and the sight of her handwriting made the find all the more moving. He said he had little left to remember her by, and although the discovery made him happy, he was also surprised by the attention the post received. When he returned to work after seeing it, he found it difficult to concentrate.Since the incident, Callum has decided he would like to continue the family’s idea as a tradition when he buys another home. He plans to leave a time capsule there, giving any future tenants the chance to find a message from the people who once lived in the property.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Israel’s Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu’s party of stalling coalition talks
articles.summary: Yashar party chief says Likud wants to drag Israel into another election under the outgoing government.
articles.body:
Gadi Eisenkot has accused the Likud party of caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of stalling coalition talks in a bid to bring about new elections.

Following the October 27 election, the leader of the centrist Yashar party has been tapped by Israel’s president to form a new government but has so far struggled to put together a ruling coalition.

He has until December 6 to form a government to replace Netanyahu. The deadline can be extended by 14 days.

The election failed to deliver a clear majority for either bloc. Eisenkot and his presumed partners won 48 seats, well short of a majority in the 120-seat parliament.

Netanyahu and his traditional alliance of far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties won 53 seats, also short of a majority.

The Yashar party has so far agreed coalition deals with the left-leaning Democrats party and the right-wing Israel Beiteinu party.

Together, they have a combined total of 36 MPs – still short of the 61 needed for a parliamentary majority.

Yashar negotiators have also held talks with Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party over the possibility of forming a national unity government involving both parties – without any breakthrough.

“Likud, for its part, was unwilling to compromise and, over two weeks, refused to put a single concrete proposal on the table,” Eisenkot said in a statement on Friday.

“Their conduct points to an effort to run down the clock until the mandate expires, split the Change bloc and drag Israel into another election under the outgoing government,” he added.

Eisenkot’s wide-ranging camp has faced divisions on whether to forge alliances with ultra-Orthodox parties or the Arab-majority lists, or whether to form a unity government with Likud.

“We are approaching a moment of decision,” Eisenkot said.

“The question is whether Likud will engage in serious negotiations and commit to a partnership that requires compromise or keep up appearances and continue to stall,” he added, while maintaining that he was still open to talks if Likud was “genuinely prepared to change course”.

Likud accused Eisenkot of working to form a “dangerous left-wing government” but nonetheless said it would still be open to a unity government.

articles.title: Aurigny flight problems throttling Alderney, islanders say
articles.summary: Residents say they are frustrated by airline's timetable changes and service disruption.
articles.body:
Cancellations and delays to Aurigny's flights caused by staff shortages and weather are "throttling Alderney", a businessman said.

Giles Woodhouse, who is head of sales for clothing brand Gym Plus Coffee, said he felt "total exasperation" by the disruption.

His comments came as the airline announced it would prioritise services to Alderney in December and January , reducing flights to Southampton to two days a week.

Aurigny's chief commercial officer Philip Saunders said the issues were "quite unacceptable" and apologised to customers. Skybus, which has a partnership with Aurigny for Alderney flights, has been approached for comment.

Woodhouse said the issues had been "hugely significant" and meant travellers had to spend "the best part of the day in Guernsey if they were re-routed".

"It means there is a constant issue of whether you are going to get away," Woodhouse added.

"At the moment you have absolutely no guarantee whether you're going to get away."

Resident Jo Woodnutt said the delays have had an impact.

"It massively harms how people see Alderney and how people think about Alderney as a place they want to go," Woodnutt said.

Ian Corder said the Alderney to Southampton route was "a vital route" and he used it for business and to see family.

The island resident said reducing the number of routes to Southampton would cause delays as "having to go by Guernsey takes longer".

Corder said it would also affect his plans to spend Christmas with family as he had been told flights "are now not available".

He said the Southampton route was important as it brought many visitors to the island.

Saunders told the BBC the timetable changes for December and January were designed to "best protect" the lifeline route to Alderney after Skybus said it only had "one set of available crew for this time".

Saunders said: "The intention for this is to be a short-time measure and the airline remains completely committed to Southampton services in the long-term."

articles.title: Did NIL really 'level the playing field' in recruiting? The answer is more complicated than you think
articles.summary: The Miami Hurricanes landed five-star edge rusher DJ Jacobs after his Ohio State decommit, giving them seven five-star commits in the 2027 class.
articles.body: With how off the rails this college football season has been at times, it's easy to forget that one of the most important days in the sport is quickly approaching. That's right, folks! In less than a week, National Early Signing Day will hit us, seemingly out of the blue. Many fans seem to think that recruiting doesn't matter now that the transfer portal is as rampant as it is now, but championship programs are still built through elite recruiting. HIGH SCHOOL RECRUIT FLIPS COMMITMENT FROM COLORADO TO MISSISSIPPI STATE BACK TO COLORADO IN 30—HOUR SPAN Speaking of elite recruiting, the Miami Hurricanes pulled off another coup in the realm of talent acquisition by landing DJ Jacobs, a five-star edge rusher fresh off of decommitting from Ohio State. If you're keeping track at home, that is Miami's seventh five-star commit in the 2027 recruiting cycle, according to the 247Sports composite rankings. FIVE-STAR EDGE RUSHER POSTS ON SOCIAL MEDIA HOW MUCH HE LOVES LSU, FLIPS TO MIAMI MERE HOURS LATER The Canes now have a signing class to rival the likes of some of Nick Saban's best hauls while coaching Alabama. When the NIL era began in earnest in 2022, the rallying cry for those in favor was that this would mark the end of teams building "super classes." A leveling of the playing field, so to speak. With signing day just five days from now, we can look at the 2027 class in terms of being a nearly finished product and assess whether that's really the case. GEORGIA FOOTBALL'S FALL FROM GRACE IN A POST-NIL ERA: DEBUNKING A LONGSTANDING NARRATIVE If you go back to the 2021 signing class - the year before it's widely agreed upon that NIL was introduced - you will see some familiar faces at the top of the heap. Most notably, Alabama, with a class that looks eerily similar to Miami's 2027 stockpile. Both teams have seven five-stars each to their name, with the Crimson Tide having two more signees total than Miami's 25 commits this year. If you look directly below that, though, you'll see some changes. Ohio State's 2021 signing class was equally as stacked as both Bama's that year and Miami's is for the 2027 cycle, with another seven five-stars in the fold. That's 14 five-star prospects split between two programs, nearly half of the entire allotment in a given cycle (most classes have roughly 32 five-stars in any given year). In 2027, that number is stretched out a bit more, with the top five teams holding 15 five-star commits. Other than Miami's nearly historic haul, Notre Dame has three five-stars, followed by Texas A&M with two, Oregon with one, and then Florida with another two rounding out the top-five. What is interesting to see, however, is that five of the top ten classes have at least three five-star prospects in their signing class. In 2021, that number was four teams, all of which resided in the top five. So, the talent is proliferating somewhat, just not as much as most people would lead you to believe. And how about those "usual suspects" that everyone sees in the top ten year after year? Surely, NIL has given more non-traditional recruiting powers a seat at the table, right? Well, yes and no. While Alabama, LSU, and Clemson went from top-five classes in 2021 to on the outside of the top ten in 2027, you'll still see plenty of familiar faces dominating the recruiting rankings. You still have perennial "offseason champs" like Ohio State, Texas, Oregon, and Georgia well represented in the top ten, however, it looks a little different this time around. Take the Bulldogs, for instance. articles.title: Rodrigo Duterte: Why former Philippine president is on trial before ICC at The Hague
articles.body:
Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte is going on trial for alleged crimes against humanity before the International Criminal Court at The Hague.

The case against the 81-year-old stems from his bloody war on drugs in which thousands of people were killed. He is the first Asian leader to be indicted by the ICC - and, if found guilty, would be the first former head of state or government to be convicted there.

Duterte's trial is seen as a litmus test for the court of last resort designed to hold the most powerful to account when domestic courts are unable or unwilling to do so.

Here is what you need to know about the trial.

Duterte was president of the Philippines from 2016 to 2022. He swept to power promising to eradicate street crime by cracking down on illegal drugs. He had built a reputation for being tough against crime as mayor of Davao, a sprawling southern metropolis, and said peace and order were necessary to spur investment.

Despite his contentious legacy, his strongman style proved hugely popular in a country with rampant drug problems. Duterte cast himself as a political outsider, and promised to champion the interest of Filipinos in the provinces who felt marginalised by Manila's elite.

Duterte is also notorious for his shocking rhetoric. He made sexist remarks, cursed the late Pope Francis and former US president Barack Obama, and once compared himself to Hitler.

He has remained unapologetic about his drug war over the years, saying in a video filmed as he was being taken to The Hague: "What is the law and what is the crime that I committed?"

Despite being in jail overseas, he remains popular, especially in Davao where he won the 2025 mayoral race by a landslide.

He heads a powerful political family. His daughter, Sara, is the current Philippines vice-president, while his son, Sebastian, is vice-mayor of Davao, currently serving as acting mayor. His eldest son Paolo is a congressman.

Duterte is charged with three counts of murder and attempted murder, as well as other offences between 1 November 2011 and 16 March 2019.

This straddles his last years as mayor of Davao and the first half of his presidency. The trial will tackle dozens of cases that the court says are representative of how Duterte used death squads to target drug users and sellers.

As president, Duterte openly encouraged the police to shoot and kill suspected drug dealers and users. The killings, which often involved people being gunned down on the streets or in alleys by unidentified men, sparked outrage.

Human rights monitors say the campaign targeted small-time pushers from the country's urban poor, while failing to bring big-time dealers and kingpins to justice. They also say suspects were summarily executed.

The true toll will never be known, although some rights groups believe as many as 30,000 people were killed in the campaign. One of the bloodiest nights of the campaign occured in August 2017 when 32 suspects were killed overnight in Bulacan, a Manila suburb.

Duterte has denied the allegations - condemning the charges against him as "an outrageous lie" - as have his officials. The police have always insisted that they killed only in self-defence.

As president, Duterte was immune from prosecution. When his term ended, his family wielded considerable political power.

For a time, his family had an alliance with his successor, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr, who ran with Sara Duterte as his vice-president. Marcos said he would not allow the ICC to arrest his predecessor.

But then the Marcos-Duterte alliance started to unravel soon after the 2022 elections, as the two families pursued divergent political agendas. Sara Duterte, widely seen as Marcos' likely successor, found herself the subject of corruption investigations. Duterte's allies then started criticising Marcos.

Marcos eventually changed his stance and allowed the ICC to arrest Duterte at Manila airport in March 2025, as the former leader returned home from Hong Kong.

The pace at which Duterte was served an arrest warrant and extradited underlined how the political winds had shifted.

What started as an airport standoff in the morning ended in a former leader once considered untouchable being flown on a Gulfstream jet to The Hague.

For the Philippines, it will offer a chance for the families of those who died in the drug war to finally be heard. Many have chosen to remain silent for years as Duterte and his allies remained in power.

Some of the widows and orphans are attending the opening of the trial on 30 November.

It will also decide the fate of one its most powerful dynasties, at a time when its high-stakes feud with a rival nears its climax.

The trial comes as Sara Duterte's impeachment trial for alleged corruption is just weeks from conclusion. If convicted, she will be disqualified from running for president in 2028.

For the ICC, the Duterte case is a test of the court's ability to function in an increasingly polarised geopolitical climate.

Duterte's headline-making arrival at The Hague last year was a much-needed win for the ICC.

It had issued two high-profile arrest warrants, one for Russian President Vladimir Putin, and another for Israel's then prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu over the war in Gaza. However to date neither warrant has been enforced.

The trial will open on 30 November at 10:00 local time (09:00 GMT).

First, the judges will ask Duterte if he understands the nature of the charges and if he pleads guilty or not guilty.

Then, the prosecution and legal representatives of the victims will give opening statements. The defence will also be allowed to deliver a statement if it wishes to.

The first prosecution witness will be presented after the opening statements. The defence will present its witnesses after the prosecution.

Public livestreams of the trial will have a 30-minute delay.

We do not know. The ICC only says it will render a judgment "within a reasonable amount of time".

For a conviction, the charges must be proven "beyond reasonable doubt".

It could take years before a final judgment.

articles.title: A Louisiana mother deposited $623,274 in asbestos settlement money 12 days before she died; her husband took control of the funds, and a court has now awarded three of their children more than $301,000
articles.summary: A Louisiana man took control of his dying wife's $623,274 asbestos settlement money, and now he has lost an appeal brought by three of their children
articles.body: A Louisiana man took control of his dying wife's $623,274 asbestos settlement money, and now he has lost an appeal brought by three of their children after a court ruled the money stayed their mother's separate property and should not have moved into his own accounts. The Louisiana Court of Appeal, Fifth Circuit, overturned a lower court ruling that had thrown out the children's claims against their father, Lionel Adams Sr., ruling for Lionel Adams Jr., Jonique R. Johnson and Brandy A. Lewis after finding their mother, Ora Jean Adams, had not finished making a valid legal gift of the settlement cash to her husband before she died. In its 25 November 2026 ruling, the appeals court told Lionel Adams Sr. to pay the three children more than $301,000 in total, centered on two settlement checks made out only to Ora Jean Adams that she put in her savings account just 12 days before she died, raising the question of whether putting her husband's name on the bank accounts gave him ownership of the cash or just let him use it. According to the court's ruling, the settlement money came to $623,274.40, and Ora Jean Adams died on 22 November 2022, without leaving a will.Settlement money deposited shortly before her deathAccording to the court's account of the case, Ora Jean Adams got two checks in early November 2022 after settling an asbestos claim, with the bigger check for $621,799.40 and the second for $1,475, both written only to her and signed over in her name. On 10 November 2022, she put the money into her savings account at Total Choice Federal Credit Union, and a member service agreement signed that day also added her husband as a joint owner on her personal checking and savings accounts. The pair had been married over 40 years but kept separate bank accounts, and their children told the court their mother had always kept her money separate from their father. Ora Jean was very sick and getting chemotherapy at that time, and she died on 22 November, just 12 days after the deposit, with no will, while the court noted that the settlement cash was clearly her separate property.Children said their mother wanted to share the moneyDuring the court case, the three siblings shared talks in which their mother spoke about what she wanted done with the settlement cash. Brandy Lewis had lived in a camper in her parents' yard for about a year after a hurricane, testified that she helped care for her mother during the last year of her life, and often helped with doctor visits, chores and other needs while Ora Jean went through chemotherapy, telling the court her mother never said she meant to give all the settlement money to her husband and instead talked about making sure her children were cared for.Brandy also shared what happened around the trip to the bank, testifying that her father got mad when her mother first would not go to the bank to deposit the checks, called Brandy and her sister, Jonique, and said: “Can you get your stupid ass mama to go to the bank and deposit the check because if not the State is going to take it.” Brandy said her mother felt a lot of pain and needed help sitting, standing and getting dressed, pulled away and said, “let the State take it” when first urged to go, agreed to go after that, and did not have Brandy go with them to the bank because her father did not want her accompanying them even though he had asked her to talk her mother into making the deposit, while neither parent said Ora Jean had chosen to give her husband the whole settlement when they got back. Jonique Johnson gave similar testimony, saying her mother had talked about splitting the money evenly among her children, wanted her grandchildren to get some too, and did not mean to leave her husband out of getting anything while wanting the money shared across the family, and their brother, Lionel Adams Jr., who lived in Arizona during his mother's final illness, also testified that she had talked about sharing the money and caring for everyone.Husband claimed his wife gave him the fundsLionel Adams Sr. pushed back against his children's story and said his wife meant to give him the settlement money, telling the court the money was meant to go into his account and that his wife left him to choose what to do with it. According to his testimony, he asked her how much she wanted him to give their children, she first named $10,000, and he said, “we’ll give them more than that,” while also claiming his wife made it clear to credit union worker Tiffany Murray that she was signing the accounts over to him and saying putting his name on the accounts as a joint owner showed the money had been given to him.After his wife died, he shared some of the money with the children, with bank records showing Brandy got $25,000 on 23 November 2022 and Lionel Jr. got $22,000 on 25 November, while Jonique also testified that she got $25,000. Still, the appeals court looked closely at what happened to the money while Ora Jean was alive, and according to the ruling, Adams confirmed he did not take out money, move money, or write checks from his wife's personal bank accounts between 10 November and 22 November 2022.Court examines transfers made after her deathThe bank records became a key part of the children's claims, with the appeals ruling saying Adams paid out $245,987 from the savings account during the week after his wife died, leaving $377,287.40 of the original asbestos settlement money in the account. On 22 December 2022, he moved $426,455.95 from the savings account and another $5,146.99 from the checking account into his own savings account, making two transfers together that came to $431,602.94, which included the last $377,287.40 in settlement money plus other money that belonged to Ora Jean, leaving just $5 in her main savings account and one cent in her checking account. The three children then filed a petition asking for damages for civil conversion and unjust enrichment, arguing their father wrongly took control of property that belonged to their mother's estate. A trial took place on 13 October 2025, in the 40th Judicial District Court in St John the Baptist Parish, and on 2 February 2026, the trial court ruled for Adams Sr., deciding his wife meant to gift the money to him by adding him as a joint account holder and dismissing the children's claims with prejudice, prompting them to appeal.Appeals court explains why joint ownership was insufficientIn its 25 November ruling, the Louisiana Court of Appeal, Fifth Circuit, disagreed with how the lower court read the law, with Judge Scott U. Schlegel writing for the appeals court that Louisiana law requires a valid inter vivos donation, meaning a gift made while the giver is alive, to include a real and final transfer of ownership. The court pointed to Louisiana Civil Code Article 1468, which defines that kind of gift as a contract where someone gives up ownership of something for good in favor of another person who accepts it, and also looked at Articles 1541 and 1544, which set rules for formally accepting a gift.The judges found the money in Ora Jean's savings account was an incorporeal movable under Louisiana law, so simply adding another person as a joint account holder did not shift ownership of the funds, and explained that having the right to pull money from a joint account is not the same as owning it. It also found the member service agreement signed on 10 November was not an authentic act of donation, noted that Adams had not moved the settlement money into his own account before his wife died, and decided Ora Jean kept full power and control over the money for as long as she lived while her husband only took control of the funds after she died, so the court found the lower court got the law wrong when it treated the joint account setup as a finished gift.Three children awarded more than $301,000The appeals court also found Adams wrongly took control of his wife's property by pulling out the settlement money and moving it into his personal account after her death, and because Ora Jean died intestate, meaning with no valid will, the court ruled ownership of her estate passed to her legal heirs right when she died. Although the three plaintiffs had asked for three-fifths of the original settlement money, which came to $373,964.64, the judges set each child's share at one-fifth of the original settlement, or $124,654.88 each, before taking off what they had already received.In its final order, the court told Adams Sr. to pay:Lionel Adams Jr.: $102,654.88, after taking off the $22,000 already received.Jonique R. Johnson: $99,654.88, after taking off the $25,000 already received.Brandy A. Lewis: $99,654.88, after taking off the $25,000 already received.The total award comes to $301,964.64, plus legal interest from the date the lawsuit was filed until it is paid, and the Fifth Circuit also told Adams Sr. to pay the costs of both the original trial and the appeal, overturning the 2 February 2026 decision and putting an award for the three children in its place.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Beyond the smog: When Delhi’s lingering cough masks a silent killer
articles.summary: Delhi hospitals recorded 6,500+ lung cancer cases via RTI; doctors warn Delhi air pollution may delay diagnosis as symptoms mimic smog-related cough.
articles.body: New Delhi: A persistent cough that refuses to go away, unexplained weight loss or breathlessness that is dismissed as the effect of pollution could sometimes be signs of something far more serious. Lung cancer, often detected at an advanced stage because its early symptoms can be subtle, is emerging as a growing public health concern, particularly in cities like Delhi, where prolonged exposure to polluted air adds to the risk.Over 6,500 lung cancer cases have reportedly been recorded in Delhi’s govt hospitals over the past few years, according to figures obtained through an RTI. While the numbers do not capture the complete burden of the disease or establish how many of these cases are directly linked to pollution, they underline the need for greater awareness and timely diagnosis.Smoking remains the biggest established risk factor, but doctors warn that non-smokers are increasingly part of the concern. Passive smoking, prolonged exposure to PM2.5, occupational pollutants like asbestos and diesel exhaust, indoor pollution and genetic susceptibility can also contribute to the risk.“Pollution is also associated with an increased risk of lung cancer, but this is linked to prolonged exposure rather than exposure over a few days,” said Dr Manoj Kumar Goel, principal director and unit head of pulmonology and sleep medicine at Fortis Memorial Research Institute, Gurgaon.He pointed out that street vendors and people working in poorly ventilated industrial environments, regularly exposed to smoke, dust and toxic gases, are particularly vulnerable.Dr Abhijeet Singh, associate director and unit head, pulmonology, ShardaCare-Healthcity, also flagged air pollution as an emerging risk factor, particularly among women and non-smokers. He said the hospital has observed an increase in respiratory illnesses and highlighted that pollution exposure is not limited to outdoor environments.Dr Ankit Jain, senior consultant, medical oncology, Indraprastha Apollo Hospitals, cautioned against attributing every case to pollution. “Air pollution is a recognised risk factor for lung cancer and is an important public health concern in Delhi-NCR. However, it would be inaccurate to attribute all lung cancer cases in the region to pollution alone. Smoking, occupational exposure, family history and other individual factors must also be considered,” he said.One of the biggest challenges is recognising the symptoms. Dr Parveen Jain, senior consultant and head of oncology at Aakash Healthcare, said lung cancer symptoms are often mistaken for seasonal allergies, pollution or routine respiratory infections.A cough lasting more than three weeks, blood in sputum, unexplained weight loss, persistent chest pain, increasing breathlessness, repeated chest infections, hoarseness and unexplained fatigue are warning signs that warrant medical evaluation. “Coughing up blood is a sign that you need to see a doctor immediately,” Dr Parveen Jain said.Doctors also underscore the problem of late diagnosis. “Unfortunately, the vast majority of patients reach us at a very late stage. In Stages 1 and 2, the disease stays largely silent, often causing nothing more than a mild, intermittent cough that people easily ignore,” said Dr Mandeep Singh Malhotra, chief mentor at Art of Healing Cancer, Gurgaon.He added that some patients lose valuable time receiving symptomatic treatment or being treated for tuberculosis before consulting an oncologist.Dr Amit Upadhyay, senior consultant, medical oncology, PSRI Hospital, said over 70% of lung cancer patients walk in at Stage IV. “In Stages 1 and 2, symptoms are often absent or limited to a mild cough. By the time persistent coughing and other severe symptoms emerge, patients may have self-medicated or been misdiagnosed with conditions like tuberculosis, delaying specialist consultation and diagnosis,” he said.Doctors say low-dose CT (LDCT) screening can help detect lung cancer early in high-risk individuals, particularly those with a significant smoking history. However, Dr Parveen Jain stressed that the screening should be guided by a doctor and should not become a routine test for everyone.The treatment depends on the type and stage of cancer and may include surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, targeted therapy and immunotherapy.Dr Ankit Jain highlighted the importance of biomarker testing, which helps identify genetic changes, such as EGFR mutations and guide treatment choices.Research is also exploring how pollution may trigger cancer development. Arun Asaithambi, PhD, founder and CEO of Katamaran Industries, cited a 2023 ‘Nature’ study showing how PM2.5-induced inflammation can promote tumour development in lung cells carrying cancer-associated mutations.With pollution exposure difficult to eliminate entirely, doctors recommend avoiding tobacco, monitoring air quality, reducing exposure to indoor pollutants and seeking medical attention for persistent respiratory symptoms. The larger concern, they say, is ensuring that lung cancer is not dismissed as just another consequence of Delhi’s polluted air.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: In honor of the USDA's release of Bigfoot files, OutKick is releasing its own reader submitted stories
articles.summary: Reader-submitted Bigfoot sighting accounts surface after the USDA's "Bigfoot/Sasquatch Records" release, detailing forest encounters in Alabama and Oregon.
articles.body: The recent news of the release of three files from the U.S. Department of Agriculture's "Bigfoot/Sasquatch Records," has inspired me to release the reader-submitted stories of reported encounters with the cryptid. Like the government documents, these stories are in some cases several decades old. However, I've only been holding onto them for a few weeks. I was already eyeballing a special Thanksgiving Day release before the USDA news broke, but once it did, I knew I had to dig them up. So, in order of when they were received, here are the OutKick Bigfoot files. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS Debra writes about her Bigfoot encounter in an Alabama forest when she was a teenager: I live in Alabama and when I was 17 myself and three of my friends were riding around in Bankhead Forest when we had one jump out of the tree line in front of our car. My friend who was driving swerved up onto the side of the road and got around it and we got out of there as fast as we could. We all saw the same thing and I don’t want to ever see one again. There have been other people who have reported seeing them in the forest. Tom details seeing big red eyes during a traditional walk to a cemetery at night: Nickerson state park , family tradition was a walk to a lil cemetery and crematorium remnants in n the woods near a lil pond. At nite one flash lite I had. Deeper we went into woods the closer my kids n several high school age friends got to me. At the ponds edge I flashed a lite on the access path . We all were meet with big red eyes Two looking at us. It didn’t move or run, it was large. Because I choose a real black nite we didnt see much. I think kids n I moved back towards road then. Did go and look for tracks in mud, saw disturbance but nothing of distinction. But not deer prints either. N deer would have run off. I. Kno behaviour No longer call their after 50 years. That and another reason. Best I got. Oh. It was a bit before we all had cell phones. GROUP OF TEENAGE CAMPERS STALKED BY A GROUP OF SASQUATCHES IN IDAHO OVER MEMORIAL DAY WEEKEND Todd had his run-in during a hunting trip in Eastern Oregon: September 17th 2013, I was hunting Elk in Eastern Oregon. I had just finished up a 4-day solo backpack hunt and was waiting at my camp for my hunting buddy to get there so we could finish hunting together. He was towing his camp trailer up to camp and I remember thinking that sleeping in his camp trailer was going to much nicer than the ground I’d been on for the previous 4 nights. He had just been released from his doctor after having back surgery and he was late getting in. Once he arrived, I helped him back his trailer into position and we leveled the trailer. It was starting to get cold and dark, so we didn’t make a fire that night… Our camp is 18 miles from the nearest paved road at about 5800 foot in elevation, on a ridge, at the end of the Forest Service Road. We were the only people there and there were no other camps or hunters anywhere near us… there were no other vehicles or people up there. It began to snow a little bit about an hour after the sun went down. My hunting partner was tired from the 9-hour drive and his back was aching, so he took a prescribed muscle relaxer and went to sleep. I was sleeping on the couch for the next week and I was rolling out my sleeping bag and I sat down and sent my wife a text back home and let her know my buddy had arrived and I was in his trailer getting ready for the next morning’s hunt. It had only been snowing for a maybe an hour, so there wasn’t much accumulation… just a heavy dusting. The dead and dried grass in the area made it look like there was very little snow. While I sat there looking out the windows, it stopped snowing and the clouds parted… the bright moon light reflecting off what snow there was made it very bright outside and lit up the inside of the camp trailer somewhat. I opened the blinds on the window so I could enjoy the view. TWO LADIES, A DOG, A LIGHTHOUSE AND A POSSIBLE BIGFOOT ENCOUNTER ON A BEACH IN MICHIGAN That’s when I saw something in the window over the kitchen sink. It looked like a very hairy person. That kitchen window was about 8 feet off the ground. I saw the hair glistening and the shape of a head. For a brief second, I couldn’t believe what I saw and thought why would someone walk into some hunter’s camp at night? Then it walked past the dining table where the window was much bigger than that of the kitchen window… probably 3 feet by 4 feet wide and a little lower than the kitchen window. That’s when I saw it’s bicep, shoulder, neck, and facial profile. It never looked in the trailer but instead just walked past our camp, disappearing into the trees behind the trailer. I sat there for a few minutes replaying what I’d seen… that was no human, that was no bear. That was a Sasquatch. I’m absolutely convinced. I waited a little while longer, then grabbed my flashlight and my pistol… realizing whatever that was and being so big, that what was that little pistol going to do to that creature. I went outside anyways and couldn’t see any tracks since the tall trees next to the camp trailer blocked it from reaching the ground. I looked in the direction it went but saw nothing. It was a rough night trying to sleep after that. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE I’ve told the story the exact same way when I’m asked about that night. It’s not something I broadcast since most people would think I’m crazy, especially in my work position. I’m sure I saw what I saw. I know not everyone will agree or understand… but that was a Bigfoot! Bonnie had a Bigfoot pay her visit at her screen door: We were living in Lake County, Mi surrounded by woods. It was a very humid night so I left the sliding door and front doors open to catch a cross breeze coming off the Pere Marquette River. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! The kids and I made beds on the floor and my husband took the couch. I was right in front of the screen door. It was very early morning with just a hint of daylight. I awoke from the smell wafting through the sliding door screen and turned over to see what was causing the smell. It was very strong and pungent.....a skunky smell. There, slightly bent down looking thru the screen door....was very tall and hairy creature . It had its right hand braced on the house. I could see it's outline clearly. And the smell was similar to that of a skunk but different. For some reason, seeing a Big Foot on the other side of the screen I was laying in front of, didn't alarm me and I layed back down . My husband woke and saw the creature and shouted..."My God, what is that"? and I responded, "it's just Big Foot". I turned back around and Big Foot was gone just that quick. At the time I had two Dobermans and they didn't react at all. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP There you have it. Those are the Bigfoot stories that I received from readers a few weeks ago. Some of Africa's largest cities are sinking faster than previously thought, new research shows.

Scientists used radar imagery from the European Space Agency's Sentinel-1 satellites to map how much the land beneath 20 African coastal cities had moved.

The study found that some cities - including Lagos in Nigeria and Alexandria in Egypt - were sinking much faster than previously estimated in 2021 by the UN's climate body, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

While some causes of this sinking, or subsidence, are natural, many are the result of human activities, such as the extraction of groundwater from underneath the Earth's surface.

Lead author Oluwaseyi Dasho said the effects of subsidence "are often invisible in everyday life, but over decades they can substantially increase flood exposure".

This is because when the ground sinks it becomes lower relative to the ocean and adds to the risk of the sea level rises caused by climate change .

Seven million people, one billion buildings and $180bn (£137bn) of assets could be at flood risk by 2050, the paper estimated.

In the past, a lack of monitoring stations has prevented scientists from obtaining up-to-date localised information on subsidence in Africa, Dasho said.

But by using satellite data, the researchers from Virginia Tech were able to detect land movements as small as 1mm per year.

Senior author Manoochehr Shirzaei said Sentinel-1 satellites flew over the same region of the Earth every six to 12 days.

"[The satellite] transmits the radar signal, which hits the ground and bounces back to the satellite," the geosciences professor explained. This process is then repeated on "many revisits".

The time between sending the signal and receiving it back is recorded, with changes in this value over time revealing how much the land has moved.

The ground under Alexandria and Lagos was found to have sunk an average of 6mm and 5mm per year respectively.

If this rate continued, sea levels around Alexandria would rise 36% more by 2050 than the IPCC predicted , under the middle estimates for how much planet-warming emissions will increase.

Luanda in Angola has also sunk significantly, but other cities such as Durban in South Africa have remained stable or even risen slightly.

Shirzaei said showing where the IPCC had underestimated risks - but also where the threat had been overestimated - could help planners allocate resources more effectively.

The man-made drivers of subsidence are usually "extremely local, [which] means that we can combat them by creating local policies", Shirzaei explained.

One major cause is the increased water consumption of rapidly growing cities. Too much water being extracted from the ground can lead to the soil becoming compacted and the surface sinking.

The Aswan Dam on the Nile may also be trapping sediment upstream and preventing the replacement of sinking land in Alexandria, the study suggests.

In Lagos, the reclaiming of land from the ocean to create artificial islands and the construction of buildings on loose ground are other possible causes of subsidence.

Methods of preventing cities from sinking include supplying other water sources and growing less water-intensive crops.

"Whatever we cannot mitigate, we try to adapt to it," Shirzaei added. This could mean building flood defences or moving key infrastructure to a higher level .

The professor said developing countries had been "left out" of much of the planning for sea-level rises due to a lack of monitoring.

The techniques developed in this study could potentially be used to address the knowledge gap in other regions, such as the Pacific islands, Shirzaei suggested.

Oluwaseyi Dasho said he hoped the paper, in Science Advances, could help African governments "prepare adequately for future challenges and more importantly for the future generations".

articles.title: DHS accuses California of endangering ICE officers after bodycam shows police telling agents 'good luck'
articles.summary: Viral bodycam footage shows a Long Beach officer telling ICE agents they are on their own as rioters blocked exits during an Oct. 17 arrest in California.
articles.body: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin accused California sanctuary politicians of putting federal agents in danger after a Long Beach officer pulled out during an Oct. 17 arrest surrounded by rioters. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is blasting California's sanctuary policies after viral bodycam footage captured a Long Beach police officer leaving federal immigration agents surrounded by an angry mob, telling them, "you guys are on your own." The confrontation unfolded Oct. 17 when Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers moved in to arrest a Mexican national in Long Beach whose criminal history includes a felony domestic violence charge – a suspect local police had previously refused to hold on an ICE detainer, according to DHS. DHS DENOUNCES TX OFFICIALS FOR ALLEGEDLY PLANNING TO END COOPERATION WITH ICE In bodycam footage released by the Long Beach Police Department (LBPD), a Long Beach officer walks up to federal agents and tells them local police are leaving. LBPD said in an earlier statement that officers responded to an emergency call from ICE regarding vehicle vandalism and a detainee needing medical attention. Police said debris blocked the roadway, forcing officers to drive a bleeding, handcuffed detainee to a nearby fire station, where police removed his handcuffs so paramedics could take him to a hospital. After LBPD left the scene, some ICE agents followed officers into a secure police station parking lot and were ordered to leave, though police said agents were told they could call dispatch if they wanted an officer to respond and take a vandalism report. articles.title: U.S. opens hotline for tips about cartels, angering Mexico
articles.summary: President Claudia Sheinbaum blasted the DEA after it set up anonymous tip lines in the country, accusing American officials of interference.
articles.body:
Mexico's president has blasted the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration after it set up anonymous tip lines in the country, accusing American officials of "interference" and not doing enough to fight fentanyl and corruption inside their own borders. President Claudia Sheinbaum said Friday the country's foreign ministry has lodged a formal complaint with U.S. Ambassador Ron Johnson.

"We have made it very clear in our relationship with the United States that the relationship is one of coordination, not subordination," she said in her daily news briefing.

Sheinbaum, in harsh comments Thursday, read excerpts from a new investigation by The Associated Press revealing how the DEA allowed at least 1.4 million counterfeit fentanyl pills to go unseized as it spent eight months tracking a drug trafficking ring flooding the Southwest with deadly drugs.

"The DEA has plenty of work to do in its own country. A lot," Sheinbaum said, pointing to the AP report. "The first thing it should do is investigate corruption in the United States linked to organized crime, or what they call terrorist groups."

"It's clearly an act of interference," Sheinbaum added.

Imagine, she mused, if Mexico "opened a WhatsApp service for reporting corruption in the United States. How would the U.S. government view that?"

Sheinbaum's angry response comes less than 24 hours after DEA Administrator Terry Cole announced the tip lines on his X account, encouraging Mexicans to denounce members of criminal networks in Sinaloa state, the corrupt officials who support them and people who launder money to finance narcoterrorism.

"Your information matters. Your identity and your safety matter," Cole said, specifying that tips submitted via Signal, WhatsApp and email would be handled confidentially.

The United States has stepped up pressure on Mexico to fight the cartels and has even offered to deploy troops on Mexican soil, something Sheinbaum has ruled out while maintaining that there will be security cooperation with Washington, "but without subordination."

On Nov. 20, Mexican military forces captured drug lord Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, alias "El Chapo Isidro," a key ally of a Sinaloa cartel faction. The FBI had placed him on its list of 10 most wanted fugitives , while the U.S. State Department offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest.

The military operation o capture him tsparked panic in the region, sending civilians fleeing from erupting gunfire. Elsewhere in the state, suspected gang members reportedly erected improvised roadblocks. In clashes with security forces , 16 cartel suspects were killed, officials said, and four soldiers also died.

Mexico requested Washington's support for the operation, and the United States sent a drone to help gather information about the drug lord's whereabouts.

The U.S. has requested Meza Flores' extradition, but Mexican Attorney General Ernestina Godoy said he will be tried in Mexico.

Chapo Isidro's capture came just days after Sheinbaum met President Trump on the sidelines of a summit in Asia.

Mr. Trump, who has pushed Mexico to do more to tackle drug gangs, said Friday that the two had discussed trade and security.

The Mexican government has knocked out several cartel kingpins. Chief among them was Mexico's most powerful cartel leader , known as "El Mencho ," who was killed in February. Similar to the capture of Meza Flores, the dramatic operation resulted in a burst of violence and burning cars.

Although cooperation between the two countries went smoothly in that operation, tensions arose between Mexico and Washington in late April after federal prosecutors in New York made public a drug trafficking indictment against Sinaloa Gov. Rubén Rocha Moya , a member of Mexico's governing party. He and nine other officials were accused of collaborating with a faction of the Sinaloa cartel, which the Trump administration has designated a foreign terrorist organization.

Amid the controversy, Rocha Moya took an indefinite leave of absence, and his bank accounts in Mexico were frozen. But Mexican authorities refused to carry out the U.S. request to arrest him. Former Sinaloa Security Secretary Gerardo Mérida Sánchez surrendered to U.S. authorities in May.

DEA whistleblowers in June revealed to the AP how agents in New Mexico in recent years permitted hundreds of thousands of fentanyl pills to go unseized. At the time, the DEA denied it ever knowingly allowed the trafficking of a synthetic opioid the White House has designated a "weapon of mass destruction."

That denial, however, was further contradicted by new AP findings that the DEA permitted at least 1.4 million additional pills to be trafficked between August 2024 and April 2025 as it closed in on the largest fentanyl bust in U.S. history.

The AP based its tally on thousands of pages of court documents, investigative records, detailed wiretap reports and 12 hours of DEA surveillance footage showing dealers moving large packages of pills in plastic bins and duffel bags that passed through highly transited hotels, apartment complexes, Airbnb rentals and self-storage facilities in six states.

The Mexican president in her comments Thursday called the DEA's decision to permit fentanyl to hit the streets the "Fast and Furious of Fentanyl," a reference to the 2011 gun-walking scandal in which straw buyers smuggled some 2,000 assault weapons into Mexico with the intent of tracing the firearms to cartel leaders.

"What is the United States doing in the United States?" Sheinbaum asked. "We have a prosecutor's office here, and the Security Ministry works here. So they should pay close attention to the other side of the border."

The DEA did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Cole said a channel for submitting tips about the state of Jalisco would be made public Thursday. The state is a stronghold of the powerful Jalisco New Generation Cartel, known by its Spanish initials CJNG, which Washington also designated a terrorist organization.

Meanwhile, a veteran DEA agent also told CBS News last month the agency has contributed to the problem by allowing fentanyl pills to reach the streets.

"For three years, I've told my DEA managers that we're allowing dangerous amounts of fentanyl to hit the street, and we're doing nothing to stop it, and they didn't listen to me," DEA Special Agent David Howell told CBS News in his first television interview.
